column121: The planned flight was VFR from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 at XA:00 on November [date] 2020 in Aircraft X (Cessna 150) rented from Company. I was PIC; Person Y was the only passenger. We had previously flown Aircraft X on July [date] 2020 from ZZZ; ZZZ4; ZZZ3 and had noted that the passenger door was not closing properly -- a small gap in the upper-left corner of the window frame allowed wind to enter the cabin. The owner of the plane investigated the issue then and found that the upper window frame was bent. I assumed that the issue was fixed by an A&P mechanic after the investigation. The plane has been regularly flown by other pilots since July.On November [date] 2020; I noticed no irregularities during pre-flight. During run-up; I noticed that the gap in the passenger door was still present and was a bit bigger than I remembered it from July. I thought that the slight wind in the cabin would be unpleasant but not otherwise an issue and continued with the flight. During the take-off roll just after rotation; the passenger door swung open. Once we were stabilized on the downwind; I shut the door and reassured my passenger. However the passenger door swung open again -- the wind through the upper-left gap torqued the entire door outward and that overpowered the door latch. So I requested landing clearance from ZZZ Tower and executed a precautionary landing without any incident. I taxied back to parking; shut off the engine and investigated the passenger door. The upper window frame was flexing slightly and could be bent to snap into the correct position. I pushed the frame into the correct position; verified that the frame was now snug against all the door frame inserts and that no wind was leaking into the cabin.I took off from ZZZ around XB:00 and noted no issues this time. As we were transitioning ZZZ3 Class D airspace; my passenger noted that she heard some sound from her door. I verified that the gap in the window frame was not present and that the door was shut properly. Shortly after we flew through the Class D; my passenger also reported that she could feel cold air from near the lower-right part of her door. As we flew past the marina; the door again swung open. This time the door shook violently which caused the window also to be flung open. I requested landing clearance from ZZZ3 was given priority and then I clarified my situation. I noted that reducing the throttle helped remove the violent door shaking. I reached over to shut the door; then pulled the upper window frame back into the door inserts and then closed the window. The ATC alerted me with a low altitude warning; so I decided to ignore the door and climb 300 ft. to intercept the glide slope and fly the plane first. As I increased RPM; the door again flung open. The door was twisting and wobbling around the hinge like a sheet of paper with the hinge as a paper-clip; and either wind or resonant frequency was increasing the severity of the wobbles. My passenger held the door to dampen its shaking. The landing at ZZZ3 was without any incident; and I taxied to a maintenance shop on the field. An A&P mechanic diagnosed that the passenger door needs to be replaced entirely and that the plane was not airworthy. We drove back to ZZZ after ensuring that the owner of Aircraft X knew what had happened and where to find the plane's key.In follow-up communication with the owner; I do not believe that the plane door was inspected and fixed by an A&P mechanic in July. The owner mentioned that he adjusted the door latches and attempted to bend the window frame back into place. This 'fix' ensured that the 'door shut properly 90% of the time'. He mentioned that he drove up to ZZZ3 with a spare C150 door and replaced it -- I do not know that he is qualified to make such repairs. His name does not show up in the airmen registry as holding an A&P license. The owner also mentioned that he was checking the door occasionally and that it had clearly worsened in the lastcouple of weeks and that there is no strength left in the window frame.Based on our conversations; I believe that the owner fixed the discrepancies that pilots reported using methods that are not by the book.(1) Normalization of deviance. I should have canceled the flight after landing at ZZZ after the initial trouble with the door.(2) Normalization of deviance. Owner should have replaced the door in July; rather than waiting for the door condition to get worse and create an [issue].(3) Crew management. I should have briefed my passenger during/after the [event]. She thankfully did all the right things (e.g. dampen the door vibrations) purely on instinct.(4) Aviate & Declare. I did not use 'emergency' or 'mayday' in my communications; despite that; the ATC at ZZZ and ZZZ3 both realized that something was up and gave me priority. Kudos to them. When diverting to ZZZ3; I flew very close to the prohibited airspace near marina to minimize my flight path to the runway.(5) Pre-flight Airworthiness Check. I should have insisted on viewing the maintenance records of the airplane to verify that my previous squawks were satisfactorily addressed.

column121: Aircraft X was at ZZZ to change the Emergency/Parking Brake cable. I was on the crew that finished installing and adjusted the cable; working the adjustment of the cable. I had safe tied the two lower jam nuts below the bracket on the handle end of the cable to each other; then over the bracket to the jam nut on top of the bracket. I used the safety cable kit for this task. The brake cable being installed does not have the locking support tab to facilitate easier safety of jam nuts. On my way to work the next day as I was driving. It occurred to me that that safety cable would cut through the bracket over time due to movement of the cable as the handle is actuated. When I arrived at work I notified the supervisor of my mistake and the plane was removed from service. The manual is not very clear about how to safety this this jam nut for this location. I was using Emb-170 AMM task 32-XX-XX for my reference. [The figure] shows the technique for a nut and jam nut at location X which is not where I was working. I corrected the safety procedure of my location to illustration X and returned the aircraft to service. The task 20-XX-XX Typical safetying methods; does not cover this situation with the jam nut. It was getting close to the end of my 12hr shift and I should have thought this thru more carefully. column121: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful.  We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.

column121: While flying [my aircraft]; I experienced an engine failure approximately 15 NM prior to the destination runway while flying at approximately 2;300 feet.  I had been experiencing extreme headwinds since a refueling stop and the leg had taken me longer than I'd planned. Because of the added flight time; I was thinking about fuel; but I thought I had enough fuel to make the intended destination with minimum reserves.  The engine failure was accompanied by a lack of fuel pressure that was not remedied by turning on an electric fuel pump.  I firmly believe it was due to fuel exhaustion.  With no airports within gliding distance; I angled the plane towards the interstate; and eventually lined up on a dark area parallel to the highway and attempted a landing onto an area about 100 yards from the highway. As I approached the field; I flared; and initially landed the main wheels successfully and rolled for a couple of seconds; probably 20 yards; but as soon as the nose wheel touched the recently plowed soft dirt; it dug in.  I did not suffer any serious injuries that I'm aware of and the plane had surprisingly minor damage.  Upon checking the fuel tanks after exiting the plane; they were indeed empty.

column121: We had walked into the hanger that morning and found out that we were doing an engine change. The engine had already been removed and needed to be installed. My Supervisor was the one in charge of the operation and he had wanted us hang the engine on the FWD top mount first then the AFT mount and then the bottom FWD mount. The task has you install the AFT mount 1st and then the 2 FWD mount; but since I had worked with him before on engine installs I just followed his lead. We had got the 1st mount installed on the aircraft we ran into some trouble on the AFT mount. We had ended up damaging both the upper and lower cowling and 2 hinge fitting panels. Later I had found out that the 2 panels were supposed to be removed before the engine ever can off the plane. We ended up pulling the engine back off aircraft and on removal the engine had snapped down and had made a small nick on the FWD mount. My other Supervisor (who was working with us the whole time) was trying to tell me that the damage was no big deal when I knew that the FWD mount had no damage limits. I had ended up writing up the damage to all 3 parts that got damaged.I believe that the damage to the aircraft could have been prevented if the 2 panels had been removed and we had followed the task in order. There should also be note in the task stating that the AFT mount needs to go in 1st. I also believe that supervisors shouldn't be doing the work of the mechanics. They seem to have a time ordinated mentally over a safety one.
column123: On DATE on first shift at the ZZZ maintenance hangar; the right engine of aircraft X was being installed by the first shift maintenance crew. The individuals who performed and assisted in the task and include; myself (NAME2 RII Inspector); NAME (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME1 (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME3 (Maintenance Lead); NAME4 (Maintenance Technician); NAME5 (Maintenance Technician); NAME6 (Maintenance Technician); and NAME7 (Maintenance Technician). NAME8; Assistance Chief Inspector was also a witness to some portions of the task being performed. During the installation of the right engine the upper trans cowling 443AT; the lower trans cowling 443AB; and the upper and lower rear thrust reverser hinge line fairings 443BT and 443BB were damaged. Also there was damage to the forward engine mount on the pylon side. NAME (Maintenance Supervisor) was taking the lead on the job and operating the heavy duty forklift. Of the employees performing the task NAME had the most experience in doing this specific engine CF34-8C5 installation. NAME6 was the only technician besides NAME who had performed the specific installation task before and he had only performed it one time. Before the job started there was a safety meeting to discuss the possible dangers of the job. Everyone was assigned a position on the lifts; on the aircraft pylon; or on the ground. NAME8 present at the safety meeting and shortly thereafter I saw him from a distance talking to NAME about the task giving him some advice on how to install the engine and to make sure the task was followed exactly. Since I was on the lift and carrying out other duties I did not hear much of the conversation but it seemed more like an argument. NAME8 left the job site and we began to hoist the engine in place. NAME directed the mechanics to install the forward engine mount first because it was easier. NAME mentioned to us all that he had done at least five successful engine changes this way with no issues. At this point no one made an objection this. The two mechanics on the engine pylon; NAME4 and NAME5 aligned the forward engine thrust mount into place and torqued and safetied the nuts and bolts. They then attempted to align and fit into place the aft thrust mount. After a few minutes of trying the aft thrust mount would not fit into place. At that point myself and NAME6 double checked the manual instructions which we had on hand on the lift. We mentioned to all that the aft thrust mount should have been installed first according to the instructions the manual laid out. NAME stated that it should not matter and they proceeded to try again to fit the aft thrust mount into place. NAME3 kept saying that he thought some thing was binding where he was in the front side of the engine pylon. He mentioned this several times but because we were all in different positions around the engine we could not see was he was talking about. NAME3 asked NAME specifically if the panel 443BT is supposed to come off because it seemed like it was in the way. NAME replied that he had never seen that panel come off in his experience. They proceeded for another few minutes and then decided to remove the engine from the aircraft and put it on the stand to double check if anything was wrong with the engine mounts on the engine side. After the engine was secured on the stand. We found the above mentioned aircraft damage. A few minutes after the damage was discovered we did some more research. We found that the technicians that removed the engine the day before on second shift failed to remove panels 443BT and 443BB that are specifically mentioned in the removal task. We believe that this was the cause of the damage to the aircraft. With the panels installed there was not enough room to position the engine in place correctly. As an R.I.I. I rejected the installation in the maintenance software program and the maintenance staff asked for engineering relief for the damage. NAME then refused to sign the AMM task even though he took the lead on the job and operated the engine lift thereby performing undocumented maintenance on the aircraft.There were many factors that contributed to this incident. One was a serious lack of experience with this specific task. At other airlines they have an engine installation and removal team the handles all engine changes because of the complexity of the task and the teamwork it takes to do the job with five or more individuals. Most of the tasks frequently performed at ZZZ are done individually or with one helper. Only one technician on the job had performed the task more than one time. The complexity of the task meant that all involved had to read and understand a greater amount of technical data in a short period of time. Also the order of installation instructions were not followed because the most experienced technician claimed it was easier to perform the instructions out of order safely. Human factors also was a cause of this incident. The supervisor taking the lead on the job; NAME; has a reputation at ZZZ for being cocky and having a know it all 'one up you' personality. I have noticed that he has a condescending leadership style and likes to be condescending to his employees to make himself look good. Rather than train his people and build his employees up he would rather tear them down to make himself look better. I have been at Company almost six years and unfortunately Company management is full of people like NAME. I believe this creates a work environment that is intimidating and detrimental to open communication. People like NAME create a 'shame' environment where people are afraid to speak up when something is done wrong or doesn't look right to them. This creates and enhances human error.  Failure to read and understand the entire task and remove all the panels on the list for the removal task CRJ 900 AMM 71-00-00-000-801-A02-PSA led to the 2nd shift mechanics failing to actually remove the required panels. Failure to follow the installation order of specified steps in the task may have led to error also.More training by experienced technicians on more complex and team oriented task to train inexperienced technicians. In the manuals special notes to identify where the order of installation is a must and cannot be deviated from.(example: Note - Aft Thrust mount MUST BE INSTALLED prior to forward engine mount to avoid damage to aircraft and engine.) Better Leadership training for Supervisors with less than 3 years experience to avoid the cocky and condescending 'know it all' leadership culture. Make Maintenance Supervision and leadership responsible and accountable for the maintenance they perform on all Company aircraft. No running away and only making the mechanics on the floor sign something off when the job is not done right and something is broken.

column121: Incident / Discovery: Maintenance work light / flash light found in the the nose landing gear wheel well which resulted in an air return of the aircraft.Aircraft location: Aircraft X B737-800 was located in the parking area at ZZZ Airport.Work Conditions: Night time; outside; no spot lighting or ambient lighting. Sky conditions clear. Temperature 30(s) Fahrenheit.On the night; Coworker and I were assigned to troubleshoot log X 'Unable to access APU bite' Per previous log entry of being suspect; I replaced the R735 relay in the J20 box; took us some time to locate the J20 box and the relay because the WDM and IPC were not clear on the exact location. 2-3 hours to locate on aircraft. This junction box is located behind the L/H rear pressure panel of the nose landing gear box structure. However; access was difficult to the box from the nose landing gear area due to the angle of access and aircraft height. In turn; I climbed into the E/E bay with a blue hand light; head lamp and a No. 2 Philips screw driver; maneuvered/positioned myself over the flight deck air supply duct along the left side of the nose wheel box structure to get better access to the J20 cover; Relay 735 and associated cannon plug for troubleshooting purposes. Coworker was in support from the nose landing gear wheel well to hand me various items I needed to work through the access structure.As documented in the log; the relay did not correct the issue so we continued to troubleshoot which required continuous access to the J20 box. I was mainly working from inside the E/E bay; not from the nose landing gear wheel well.As the night progressed and not finding any faults with the physical wiring; we reported to our lead where we were at. Was told that the aircraft is needed for a flight; document where we were at and close up the aircraft.We headed back out to the aircraft. When we got back to Aircraft X; I double checked the APU ECU security; checked the aft cargo bay for equipment and tools; closed the aft cargo bay door. I then proceeded into the E/E bay to secure the J20 box cover and check for security and check for tools and equipment. As I was doing this; Coworker was securing the nose landing gear wheel well pressure panel.After Coworker finished installing the panel; I went inside the flight deck to re-engage two circuit breakers and to pressurize the aircraft for the leak check of the pressure panel. Once pressurized; Lead performed the leak check of the pressure panel. When leak check was satisfactory; I depressurized the aircraft; powered down; closed the main cabin door and pulled the air stairs. Shortly after we met in the vehicle we had and began going over paper work.Coworker and I are somewhat new to avionics and have a lot to learn about the various differences between our fleet types and associated details of each. We are very capable of doing the work but would feel more comfortable to be paired with someone who is well seasoned in the avionics shop. It should be this way for anyone that is new. Since I have been in the shop; I have been paired mainly with inexperienced technicians who are learning the same way as I am; learn as you go. Common sense would dictate to pair a very experienced tech with a inexperienced tech; this promotes growth; development and prevents mistakes.I'm sorry that this unfortunate mistake took place and is an oversight I strive to never let happen; unfortunately it did. I will be much more vigilant in the future about tooling and equipment used for aircraft maintenance to make sure this will never happen on my end again.
column123: My co-worker and I received our assignment to work on the Aircraft X located [in parking]; a remote maintenance area (ZZZ). Everything was overwhelming. But all that been said; I still take a full responsibility for my action and I hope this will not repeat itself again. Thank you.

column121: This was my first flight at the controls of a tail wheel aircraft. I was in the left seat receiving flight instruction from the CFI in the right seat. A thorough pre-takeoff briefing including experience levels and positive transfer of controls was accomplished before departure.As we approached ZZZ; we briefed the fact there was a right crosswind with gusts and the appropriate actions to take regarding this. The approach was stabilized. A normal wheel landing was accomplished and the tail was successfully lowered to the ground. The left main tire failed; at which point the instructor stated 'my airplane' and I released the controls. The resulting swerve was not controllable and the airplane ground looped approximately 150 degrees; coming to rest on the runway. We immediately shut down the aircraft and exited. No propeller or wingtip contact with the runway occurred. The aircraft remained on the runway. No injuries occurred.
column123: The mission was to fly with 2 friends and give them tail wheel instruction. There was a crosswind from the right and we discussed crosswind correction and the plan. [The pilot flying] conducted the wheel landing and shortly after putting the tail down; the airplane started shaking violently. I thought this may have initially been a tail wheel shimmy; which was odd since it didn't shimmy since the tail wheel springs were replaced in month; but the airplane started veering to the left so I announced 'my controls' and corrected it with right rudder. The shaking got worse and the plane then swung around to the right and ground looped. The wings did not contact the surface and there was no prop strike. The airplane was then towed to the hangar where I worked with a mechanic to change the wheel and tire so that the plane could be moved while inside the hangar. I did identify some contributing factors. There was a strong right crosswind; it was my student's first landing; and I had previous issues with my tires slipping on grooved runways. They are 8.50 oversize tires. I do believe the left main tire went flat on landing; and with the strong crosswind and delay of taking the controls from my student; it was unrecoverable. I'm filling out this report to detail human factors issues that contributed to damage to my precious airplane; and as the investigation unfolds it will determine if there is need for additional caution when using larger tires.

column121: I was assigned to and present aboard a deadhead flight. I opted to occupy the center jumpseat of the cockpit for taxi and takeoff. At the southwest end of the ramp was a wing-walker with lighted-wands; and several other employees. As the plane approached the southwest end of the ramp; the wing-walker and other ground personnel passed out of my field-of-view and were not visible to me for the duration of the taxi; due to the visibility limitations of the jumpseat.The Captain then began the 180-degree right turn denoted by the ramp taxiway centerline. At the Captain's request; the First Officer monitored the right wing during the turn. Upon completion of the 180-degree turn; the aircraft appeared (from the jumpseat view) to be located on or near the centerline of the ramp taxiway. The Captain then requested the First Officer verify that the right wing was clear of obstacles. The First Officer turned his head far enough to the right to see the wingtip of the aircraft. He responded that the wing was clear; and that he had the wing-walker in sight.The Captain then began a left turn towards Taxiway F. The Captain's focus was on the turn. The First Officer monitored the aircraft which was giving way to us; as we [exited] the ramp. (The aircraft was approaching from the opposite direction; with its taxi-lights on; however; it had been stationary for several minutes prior to this point.) Passing through 20 degrees of left turn; a shudder was felt in the cockpit; similar to heavy braking.The Captain immediately brought the aircraft to a stop. All three of us in the cockpit made a visual inspection of the aircraft (from the cockpit.) The cause of the shudder was not readily apparent. At my request; the Captain checked the Main Body Gear Steering indications on the EICAS; to verify it was not the cause of the shudder. At that moment; (deadheading) Captain [Name] entered the cockpit and advised us that the right wingtip had separated from the aircraft.The Captain proceeded to start the APU; shut-down the engines; configure the aircraft for towing; and make contact with the ground crew. After the damage was inspected by ground [personnel]; a tow vehicle was connected. The aircraft was towed back to the parking spot; where the cargo was off loaded and the aircraft turned over to maintenance [personnel] for inspection.Immediately following the events described above; the right wingtip was discovered on the ground; adjacent to a ramp lighting tower located on the southwest end of the ramp. (This tower had passed off the right wing during the right 180-degree turn required to exit the ramp.) Ground personnel reported that the Tower appeared to have damage; in addition to the aircraft's own damage.Shudder notice after contact with obstacle.Inadequate ramp space/clearance from obstacles.Ramp space and access points need to be verified for sufficient obstacle clearance prior to operating at such location.

column121: The landing was excellent; Rollout of the aircraft was straight and smooth. When reaching for the toe brakes; I had a left brake but no right break. The toe brakes are little round pads on the top outsides of each rudder and are not easily identified with your toes even with soft sole shoes which I wear to fly in. I did not realize my foot had slipped off or was not on it properly until it was too late. The aircraft took a left direction as I was wishing to slow down. I let go of the left brake and caught it/straightened it with the right rudder. Right after I had it straight; I removed my right foot to lift it higher up to engage the right brake. The aircraft took a sharp left direction went onto the grass which with then full right rudder and the right brake did not help. The slope away from the runway is very steep and the aircraft was not able to be brought back up onto the runway; so I kept it straight and aimed at the taxiway; With the airplane tailwheel not willing to provide steering since it was on grass and the slope was still steep; the aircraft slid over the other side of the taxiway. The aircraft refused to turn right with all my efforts; so my next choice was to hit trees and or a building; so I choose to ground loop the airplane to avoid the trees and building. NO damage was done to any property including taxi signs or even lights. The aircraft came to a stop 180 degrees to the landing direction. No one was hurt in any manner since the speed was not very fast. The right gear leg collapsed as it stopped and the prop hit the grass and broke one of the tips. The engine was shut down and everything was turned off. The Runway XX is a challenging runway since there is zero room for error.

With that assessment; we accepted a ferry permit to fly back to base ZZZZ without passengers; for proper maintenance action. column121: I departed ZZZ at ZA:10 local on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1 in [a rented aircraft]. A preflight inspection at ZZZ revealed no items of concern; and the brakes responded as expected when I tested them upon first movement from the tie down spot and throughout my taxi. The weather was VMC for the duration of the flight; and the weather I picked up on the ZZZ1 ATIS 15 minutes prior to arrival was winds 320@7kts; 9SM visibility; sky clear. I informed ZZZ Approach I would take the visual approach to Runway XX; at which point they cleared me for the visual approach and handed me off to ZZZ1 Tower. Tower requested me to continue on course to fly a left base for Runway XX and report three miles west of the field. Upon my reporting three miles west of the field; they cleared me to land runway XX. Upon nearing the extended centerline; I turned 90 degrees left and aligned myself on an approximately three mile final for Runway XX while at approximately 1;200 feet MSL and 90 KIAS. I completed my final approach and before-landing checks; including pumping the brakes to check for pressure; and crossed the runway threshold at approximately 65 KIAS with 30 degrees of flaps. Immediately upon touching down; the aircraft yawed violently to the left. I applied full right rudder deflection; which somewhat arrested the left yawing and increased the radius of the turn. However; the left main wheel by that time had entered the grass adjoining the runway; further aggravating left yaw. The aircraft continued to rotate about the left wheel until it came to a stop facing approximately due east approximately 75 feet from the west edge of the runway. After ensuring there was no immediate danger of fire or structural damage; I checked the main gear tires out the windows to see if one had blown; but they appeared to be OK. I advised Tower I would try to taxi back to the runway and proceed to the ramp. Upon applying throttle; the aircraft pivoted about its pitch axis into a slight nose-down attitude; which ceased upon decreasing throttle. I tried twice more to increase throttle to induce forward movement; but the aircraft continued to pitch forward when throttle was increased and pitch backward when throttle was decreased. At that point; I informed Tower I would need a tug. An airport crew came with a tug and attached a towbar to the aircraft. Upon attempting to pull the aircraft forward; the tug was not able to move it and subsequently became stuck in the ground. The airport crew then tried using a pickup truck to pull the tug while the tug pulled the aircraft; but the pickup truck became stuck. A 4wd pickup truck came and was able to remove the tug and the first pickup truck back to the runway. The airport crew used a shovel to dig the front wheel of the aircraft out of the ground; as it had become stuck during the previous attempts to taxi back onto the runway. They then attached the towbar to the 4wd pickup truck and were able to get the aircraft moving and onto the runway. I was then able to taxi the aircraft to the ramp under its own power; but noticed it had difficulty tracking in a straight line without additional brake inputs. Upon reaching the ramp; I did a quick inspection of the brake assemblies and discovered a metal-on-metal scraping noise when moving the aircraft back and forth by hand and no movement of the calipers when the toe brakes were actuated. At this point; I felt it was unsafe to continue operating the aircraft and arranged for a mechanic to inspect it the following morning. I called the owner; and he told me; 'that is why you shouldn't take that airplane places on a [weekend] afternoon - no one is around to fix it.' The mechanic inspected the brakes and found that the caliper slider pins were void of lubricant and rusted frozen; one brake lining was missing its rivets due to them rusting away; and several fasteners were loose. He replaced the linings on both slides; lubricated the assemblies; and torqued all the fasteners. I visually inspected the brakes; tested them on the ramp and during runup; and was satisfied that the aircraft was safe to operate. I departed ZZZ1 and had an uneventful IFR flight and landing back at ZZZ.In the future; I will add more thorough visual inspection of the brake assemblies to my preflight inspections; along with checking to make sure the calipers move when the brakes are actuated. I will also land prepared for a problem such as stuck brake; blown tire; or FOD and be more ready to immediately lift back off if safe to do so.

column121: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX; exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C; and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate; we started to slowly taxi; when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us; and crossed Runway XX; which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs; and in fact; Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED'; so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless; we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate; and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller; but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1; so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork'; and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong; but it's better to be safe and proactive; and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times); the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time; we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So; probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen; but regardless; in the future; will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent; and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions; where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground; or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller); and instead treat it just like a busy airport.

column121: Description of Event: The aircraft with PIC as above and one passenger was returning to ZZZ from a 1-hour cross-country flight that originated at ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful in VFR weather; with altitude from 2;000 feet to 1;600 feet after takeoff and climbout until approach. Flight path was as depicted in the charted course; following VFR altitude restrictions as required within ZZZ2 Mode C airspace; and with ADS-B Out active on 1200 a required. Visibility was observed to be 10+ miles with a solid cloud cover (overcast) at 9;000-12;000 feet. Winds were variable 6-9 knots at approximately 230-260 degrees from surface to flight altitude. Within 10 nm on the approach to ZZZ on a vector of 220; while monitoring ZZZ voice radio on 123.00; little traffic within the airport operations area was observed or noted on the radio. At approximately 8 nm from ZZZ; an inbound aircraft was announced on my ForeFlight display through the ADS-B In signal at my 7 o'clock; 400 feet below and overtaking. That Cessna 152 pilot announced his intention for a straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX. Communicated directly with that PIC and told him that we would slow down to distance behind him on my own straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX; since he already had a 25+ mph speed advantage. Within 2 minutes; the Cessna 152 had passed us by on our left side and descended ahead of us to line up for Runway XX. In the process; I lost visual contact with that aircraft; and since there was no other traffic in the area; and ForeFlight did not show a blip for its position; I decided to perform a slight S-turn to the left to further delay our landing until the 152 announced he was clear of Runway XX. At approximately 4 nm from the threshold; with our speed down to 62 mph (58 mph Ground Speed); the Cessna 152 PIC announced 'clear of Runway  XX ZZZ'; after which I immediately announced a straight-in approach for Runway XX ZZZ and began to adjust our speed and trim to line up with the two VASI lights on the glide path. At approximately 2 nm; we were high (two white lights) but gradually settled to a nominal (white/red) glide slope on the final approach. We completed visual and verbal cockpit checks and I glanced outboard at the right Flaperon position (there being no flap setting indicator in this CH750 STOL; and no stall warning annunciation); but did not notice anything incorrect; even though I had earlier made a mental note that we would be making a flaps-up; standard landing instead of the full-flaps; STOL landings I usually make. We settled slightly low of nominal (two red lights) as we approached the threshold and at that moment; I made a mental 'flip' or attitude adjustment that we were about to land STOL; and I decreased power for a short-field landing. Our sink rate increased; but mentally; I still had confidence that the STOL nose-up attitude was safe; and did not add power but instead retarded it to idle as we crossed the threshold of Runway XX. Without flaps; our stall speed was 48 mph instead of 42 mph; and we stalled out at approximately 12' above the numbers and fell in a slightly nose-high attitude until impacting on the main and then nose gear. The aircraft bounced up and then impacted slightly nose-down; collapsing the nose strut; blowing out the nose tire; and stopping the engine as the fiberglass prop blades impacted and flexibly shattered.We immediately checked for fuel leaks even though the aircraft came to rest tail-high. I switched off the ignition and removed the key; exited the cockpit; checked again for fuel leaks (none); then shut down the avionics manually with the master switch; and turned the Fuel Selector valve to OFF. After ascertaining that the aircraft was not an immediate hazard and that both Pilot and Passenger were able to move about without difficulty; we called other airport residents; and cleared the CH750 from Runway XX.Conclusion: In summation; distracted flying due to traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement resulting in a stall upon landing flare with flaps retracted and subsequent nose gear collapse without injuries.

column121: During preflight in bitterly cold ZZZ; the FO (First Officer) completed the walk around as snow began to fall. The flaps were full down from the previous flight. She came to the cockpit and informed me that the flaps were clear of debris and asked if we should retract them for the deicing we would need after start. I agreed we should; and we did. Unbeknownst to us; the fueling of the aircraft began during this time and we didn't notice as we retracted the flaps. Just before pushback; ramp informed us that Maintenance was checking the refueling door on the wing; as it was damaged. This was our first indication that we may have damaged the door during flap retraction. Later on; maintenance personnel came to the flight deck and told us of the problem and that we would be swapping aircraft due to this.Cold weather operations; delayed fueling; miscommunication and worsening weather all contributed to this event.Don't touch the flap handle until all preflight items are complete before pushback regardless of weather conditions.

column121: This was my third solo XC (Cross Country). Flight planning was approved by the instructor. Weather and NOTAMs were reviewed by both myself and instructor and flight was deemed safe to proceed. There were no NOTAMs or field condition reports for the destination airport. One pattern was flown at departure airport with an instructor to update currency prior to departure of solo flight. Takeoff; climb; en route; and descent were uneventful. During a visual approach to Runway 02 at the uncontrolled airport; I noticed patchy snow on the runway. I noticed other aircraft had landed recently. I was expecting a normal landing to a touch and go. ASOS indicated the winds were from the northwest at 8 kts. I touched down on centerline at 67 kts. Before I set the nose down; the aircraft started veering to the left. I made the attempt to correct and the airplane continued to slide to the left. I believe due to the unresponsiveness of my control inputs; I was on ice. I made the decision to full stop and applied brakes. The aircraft continued to slide on the icy portion of the runway with no response to my braking or control inputs. The aircraft struck a snow bank on the left side of the runway. The aircraft tipped forward and to the right; resulting in damage to the propeller and the right wingtip. I'm not sure if this is a reportable incident/accident at this time. The following day; a NOTAM was issued for 30 PCT patchy snow and ice.	I believe I landed on a patch of ice. There were no NOTAMs published at the time of my departure. Had a NOTAM been published for wintery conditions; I would not have attempted a solo XC to this airport. I have not yet been trained to land in wintery conditions. Based on previous landing markings on the snow in the runway; I assumed it was safe to land. My relative inexperience resulted in not recognizing the ice under the snow. I should've gone around. In the future; I will take a harder look at my experience level and the conditions present in order to make a better decision. I have learned a valuable lesson to always err on the side of caution.

column121: There were snow drifts on the taxiway and runway.  Due to the snow; upon climb out; pilots side landing gear door would not close completely.  I cycled the gear several times to try and clear the snow to allow the gear to close fully.  We were unsuccessful getting the gear to close; so I decided to land and see if we could resolve the issue.  Feeling the departure airport was unsafe due to the runway conditions; I decided to divert to ZZZ1 to assess the situation.  I am familiar with the airport and they have a Tower and other facilities.  Roughly 20-30 minutes after ATC gave us our clearance to ZZZ1 (while we were at FL270); there was an explosion like sound and all cabin pressure immediately departed.  This blow out knocked off all of our headsets.  Understanding that we had a cabin de-presserization; I immediately pulled the power back to idle; dropped the landing gear and nosed the plane over for rapid descent.  Once we were going down; I changed our squawk to 7700 (knowing that this was our only form of communication with the outside world); set the autopilot to level off at 12;500 feet and re-engaged the autopilot in case I were to black out.  I didn't grab for my oxygen mask because at the time we were already coming down at a rate of over 8;000 ft/min and the wind/cold and just chaotic nature of the cabin; I didn't feel comfortable taking my hands off of the controls.  I also didn't go for my headset for similar reasons; as well as there being so much noise; I knew there would be no way for me to hear ATC let alone they be able to hear me. After we were able to level off at 12;500 feet; I looked for the closest airport (ZZZ2); brought up their weather and loaded the approach we wanted and turned to the appropriate heading.  I opened the inertial separator; turned on our landing and wigwag lights and decided to leave the gear down for the remainder of the flight.  I didn't want to accidentally add any other complications to our situation.  After what seemed like the longest approach in history; we finally touched down safely at ZZZ2; where I taxied the plane to the already waiting emergency vehicles.

column121: Aircraft is non-electrical with no starter; and based at a private airpark home.  Aircraft was tied down at tail and triple chocked. Preflighted and prepared for a normal start and flight. Normal start; but as I was walking around wing to the cockpit engine power increased more quickly than expected after start. I was unable to reach the cockpit to shut the engine down before the chocks gave way followed by the tiedown stake pulling out of the ground. Aircraft traveled unoccupied down sloping yard and hit a ditch coming to rest on the taxiway; resulting in landing gear damage and propeller striking ground and pavement and engine shutdown. No injuries or property damage occurred. In retrospect I have always been careful to secure the aircraft for start correctly with triple chocks and tie down. It's possible; on this start; I may not have tightened the throttle friction lock fully which may have allowed the throttle position to travel partially forward after start. The chocks in front of all three tires started to strain; then failed and the aircraft rolled forward as I was moving around the wing. The last available restraint was a tiedown at the tailwheel position. Momentum and some slack in the tie down rope caused the tiedown stake to pull loose from the ground as the slack was taken up. The downhill slope of the yard added to the acceleration before impact with the ditch. I should have double checked the throttle setting and friction lock to make sure that throttle position would not change. The increase in power would not have happened.

column121: I was enroute to ILM. As I began my descent into the Wilmington terminal area the ATIS and Approach Controller indicated ILS Runway 06Z was the approach in use. Weather was reported as 400 overcast and one mile visibility. Winds 030 degrees at 4 knots. A cold front and convective activity was approaching the airport and I requested a short vector to final. I was cleared for the approach and began my descent. I ended up too high on the approach and executed a missed approach at minimums. As I was being vectored back for another approach I was advised that the aircraft following me also executed a missed approach due to being too high. I looked at the wind vector on my PFD and realized that I had a 50 knot tailwind at 1;500 feet on my last approach. I advised the Controller about the strong winds at altitude and asked if Runway 6 was still the best runway.I also asked the Controller if he had any real time winds on the ground and was reminded that the Tower was closed; he would try to get me an update from the automatic reporting system. I was told that the automatic reporting system still indicated winds out of the NE (northeast) at 11 knots. I continued for a second approach but at 700 feet AGL my wind vector was showing a 50 knot tailwind and my groundspeed confirmed that. I deemed it unsafe to land and executed another missed approach.The Controller suggested ZZZ as an alternate. I began vectors to an approach to RNAV GPS Runway XX. I quickly realized that I would have the same 50 knot tailwind situation at ZZZ and began questioning the Controller about any real time wind information on the ground. He said the only info he had still indicated winds on the ground were out of the NE about 7 knot. He said the convective activity situation at Wilmington was improving and asked if I would like to go back for another approach. I was beginning vectors to another ILS Approach 06Z. I was still seeing the same 50 knot winds at altitude and began doubting the wind reports on the ground. I asked for an approach to Runway 24. I was cleared for the RNAV approach 24. As I was descending on final approach; I had a 50 knot head wind at 1;000 feet.When I reached minimums and began to go visual; I encountered a windshear. I increased power to MCT (Max Continuous Thrust) trying to climb out; but to no avail. As I was continuing to recover from the windshear; my landing gear contacted a treetop about 1/4 mile from the runway. At this point I deemed the safest course of action was to continue to land. I made a normal landing to a full stop; turned off the runway and taxied to the FBO. After exiting the airplane minor damage was noted. At this point the winds on the ground had shifted to the SW (southwest)) and were gusting to 35 kts indicating to me that I had landed during frontal passage.The biggest contributing factor to safety I noted; was the lack of any real time winds on the ground. If I had real time wind data from the Controller as I was conducting my approach; I would have been advised of the wind shift occurring; and might have been able to take preventive action before I encountered the windshear. My recommendation is to not have a system that solely relies on the automatic reporting system which is not real time. I would have each Approach Control have the ability to see and give real time winds just as an operating Tower would have.

column121: Upon arrival at ZZZ Maintenance notified us that there were multiple damaged fan blades in the number 1 engine. While we do not know when or how this occurred; we can only guess that it was due to snow/ice ingestion on takeoff roll; improper de-icing and inspection of engine inlets prior to engine start; or de-icing prior to takeoff. While there was no active precipitation; upon arrival at the aircraft; the crew noted snow and ice on the aircraft to include in the engine inlets. Per [company] procedures; after the doors were closed; before blockout; the crew call Ramp to have engines cleared. The clearing crew showed up. The Tug Driver noted them moving around the aircraft and appeared to be clearing engines. They left shortly thereafter; and we confirmed with Ramp Tower that the clearing and inspection had been logged complete. After push back onto taxi; we noted that the taxi lane had not been completely plowed. There was a large snow berm; approximately 2 ft. high about 10 ft. left of centerline; which converged toward centerline all the way until Taxiway XX. After some discussion with Tower and the Pushback Crew; we opted to have plows come and clear an area in front of us; that they could pull us to clear of the berm before engine start to avoid ingestion. Engine start was slow; even for Pratt & Whitney; but no starter or engine limitations were exceeded. N1 started around 20-25%; well below the 40% limit. After engine start anti-ice was turned on due to temp/dew point spread. We taxied on cleared pavement to the de-ice area. The taxi took less than 15 minutes so no engine clearing was used. During de-ice we noticed B777 push back out of a gate on [taxiway XX]. It was pushed back through a berm of snow and ice. After de-ice we taxied and took off after this B777. It is possible that the B777 had some snow/ice on its trucks that was deposited on the runway on takeoff. From de-ice; we taxied to Runway XX. The turn from Taxiway XY onto Taxiway XZ could have been cleared of snow better; but the turn was made using minimal thrust. It is possible that some compact snow or ice was ingested here; however; once cleared for takeoff; we did a 30 second engine clearing procedure and all engine instruments appeared normal. After takeoff; the Captain mentioned a rumble; which sounded like it was coming from a pack. It was faint enough; that we didn't feel it was an issue; as all packs checked out normal. Later on climb out the number 3 engine EVM fluctuated up to 5.0; then back down to normal ranges only slightly above the other two engines. The captain sent a message to [Operations} asking about engine telemetry; and we were advised it was good; so we decided to press on.

column121: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ; for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel; it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2; a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM; until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal; then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day; as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried; however I did complete the retest task per the AMM; with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event; I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.

column121: I am a student pilot that was performing my initial solo cross country.  I had safely completed the initial leg; and was returning to ZZZ.  On final; in the flare; I experienced an unanticipated crosswind gust; which resulted in the airplane dropping suddenly and causing a hard landing on the left main gear.  I applied full power to go around and re-attempt the landing.  I noticed that the airplane was yawing more than usual and recognized the airplane was operating in an abnormal condition.  Shortly thereafter; I heard a radio call that a landing gear was visible on the runway at which point I realized that I had lost my left main gear.  I continued to fly the traffic pattern under radio guidance from a CFI who was on the ground while I burned fuel and prepared for an emergency landing.  On final; under instruction from the CFI; I cut all fuel and powered down the aircraft; while continuing to fly the airplane to a landing. I landed on the right main gear and the aircraft settled to the ground ultimately skidding on in its belly as it made contact with the runway surface.  Due to the lack of directional control from only having the right main gear; the aircraft skidded left off the runway and came to rest in the grass left of the runway surface. I was able to exit the aircraft safely with no physical injuries. Following the event; I was interviewed by an Aviation Safety Inspector from the CITY Flight Standards Office and discussed the details shared above in its entirety.

column121: Local training flight from ZZZ. PIC (Pilot-in-Command) was a highly experienced glider pilot receiving a dual flight from this reporter (CFI-Gliders) to demonstrate proficiency for becoming a 'mentor pilot' for this glider club. This was his second flight of this evolution and he had requested to do a simulated rope break. The flight was briefed with the tow pilot before takeoff and also between both pilots in the glider. The takeoff was an aero-tow behind the club tow aircraft and was uneventful. At 300-350 ft. AGL the release was actuated and the glider made an uneventful turn toward the runway end with ample altitude and airspeed. In the course of the approach the pilot-flying extended the air brakes and failed to retract them at an appropriate time to allow adequate remaining altitude for a normal landing on the runway. The pilot-not flying immediately told the pilot-flying to close the air brakes and such action by the pilot-flying was delayed until the pilot-not flying immediately closed the air brakes to avoid collision with the embankment at a lower level. The aircraft struck the end of the runway at a slope embankment about 2 feet below the grass runway surface elevation and came to rest upright and on the grass runway landing surface. Inspection revealed a wrinkle about 6' x 12' on the left lower fuselage just forward of the main landing gear door (single wheel landing gear). No other damage was immediately apparent and both occupants were uninjured and the glider was towed back to the tie down area and disassembled. Later inspection revealed a small wrinkle; about 1/4' height; on the upper surface of each wing about 18' outboard of the wing root.The pilot-flying is commercial rated in gliders and the pilot-not flying was commercial; CFI rated in gliders.Cause: Failure of pilot-flying to maintain adequate altitude on final approach caused by mismanagement of air brakes. Failure of pilot-not flying to recognize and intervene sooner with closing the air brakes when the pilot-flying failed to do so.

column121: Shortly after takeoff we received a bird strike in our Number 1 Engine that caused considerable damage. Based on the engine vibration as well as the unusual noises coming from the aircraft; we determined it was necessary to immediately return for landing at ZZZ. I received priority with air traffic control and the First Officer continued flying the aircraft. There were no ECAM actions or QRH follow ups. Although there were high vibration indications as well as some initial fluctuations with N1; N2 and EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature); the engine parameters remained in the realm of normal. Therefore; the First Officer and myself did not see any reason for shutting the engine down in flight. We landed safely; let the airport personnel do a quick inspection of the aircraft on the taxiway and then returned to the gate.It all went fairly well. There was a startle factor with this event. But; in general we followed everything we learned in training. However; I may have delegated the re-configuring of the aircraft to the First Officer a bit too soon. He did that on his own. It was all done correctly. But; I don't remember doing the normal acceleration altitude call outs. I did all the standard communication procedures to ATC; cabin crew; passengers and Dispatch. Then; rejoined the First Officer for the approach preparation. The First Officer handled flying the aircraft as well as his communication with ATC perfectly.There is nothing that I can suggest that would prevent this from happening again. We always have to contend with the hazards associated with migratory waterfowl. Always consider that as a threat during that time of the year as well as keep a vigilant lookout.

column121: We departed ZZZ on a Part 91 leg to ZZZ1. Reaching our initial assigned altitude from approach we were given a climb to 17;000 and that's when we lost EDC2 without making any changes to anything. We were caught totally by surprise. As a result there were several alarms and aural warnings sounding that could not be silenced. That's also when we realized that we could no longer communicate through the intercom and the First Officer had zero radio communication. We communicated through hand signals and loud talking. I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg but I took controls at this point since I was the only one with radio communication. I pressed the autopilot disconnect button to ensure everything was disengaged and never made an attempt to reactivate it. I leveled at 14;000 and asked for a heading to troubleshoot and run the appropriate checklist. I announced that we had a failure of EDC2 and asked my First Officer to run the checklist. I couldn't hear any part of the checklist but he announced that the last step was to land as soon as practical.  I [requested priority handling] and asked for vectors back to ZZZ. I received a heading and a descent and [the] First Officer competed the appropriate checklists for descent and approach. On final approach during our before landing checklist we realized the gear did not indicate down. We aborted the landing and tried to see if the Tower controller could confirm if the gear was down or not. We made the first pass and he thought it was down but asked us to make one more pass with all the lights off in the Tower so they could try to get a better look. Again he said it looked like they were down. I considered calling for the emergency gear extension procedures but I felt a sense of urgency to get on the ground. There were several alarms sounding and we were still struggling to communicate. I was attempting to troubleshoot mentally but hand flying the airplane was my priority. At this point I realized I was getting overloaded and we still had no idea what had caused the failure in the first place. I was worried things could continue to get worse at any moment and I decided to land because so believed it was the safest thing to do. Just before touch down I recognized the gear was not down and I gently applied pressure on the power levers backwards against the flight idle stops to fully committed to the landing. At this point I knew a go around was dangerous. We touched down smoothly on centerline skidded down the runway. We finally came to a gentle halt just slightly off the runway in the grass. We ran the shutdown procedures and evacuated through the door where we were greeted by fire rescue. After walking away without even a scratch I discovered things were starting to come back to me that I couldn't seem to remember during flight. Details about the systems that I've learned in training that I could not dig out of my head while we were in flight. I've learned a lot about myself and how I react when the workload gets high and I know I can handle any future emergency better than this one. That being said; my First Officer and I were the only ones involved and we walked away completely unscathed.

column121: There were storms in the area; and we were given a reroute by ATC; to go south to the coast; and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer; Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight; and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I; the CP (Captain; Pilot Flying); had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out; we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280; it was smooth; so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast; ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight; and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms; had stayed within 50 NM of the coast; and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence; and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO; we agreed that flying south of our route; and staying within 50 NM of the coast; was our best option. At this time; I had my radar up; and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps; turned the seat belt sign back on; and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of; and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north; while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up; as it was only reading green. Almost instantly; we went into severe turbulence; and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes; and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence; we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us; heard a bang; and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck; we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us; it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude; at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance; to which we replied no. As previously mentioned; this happened very quickly. All in all; I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds; and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280; we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast); and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA; and asked if she was OK; to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers; which she did. There were no injuries; and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard; we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing; both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around; noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike; but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence; Lightning strike; and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event; with the PF using the radar; and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time; with ATC advising us of going south of the cells; as opposed to north; the decision; at the time; to go south was the correct one. That being said; I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells; but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event; by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However; the radar has its limitation; especially considering they are older pieces of equipment; and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells; of which we hit. After the event; ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately; I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast; but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally; I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate; multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew; checking that we were OK; and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values; of which we stand for; and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.

column121: I was practicing air taxiing and quick stops with a 31-hour student pilot on a taxiway. During the recovery phase of the quick stop; the student did not raise enough collective to arrest the descent. I took controls at around 30 feet AGL and increased the collective to our 5-minute limit; but we continued to descend and impacted the ground hard enough to spread the skids. A piece of non-structural sheet metal detached from the underside of the helicopter and landed beside the taxiway. I reported what happened to the tower and they sent someone to retrieve the sheet metal. I flew the helicopter back to the flight school's ramp and did not observe any damage other than the spread skids. I should have taken the controls earlier and not allowed the descent rate to develop to an unrecoverable state. I was trying to talk the student through the correct control inputs when I should have just abandoned the maneuver and recovered.

column121: Pushback was delayed due to catering (and vehicles impeding the catering truck from approaching the aircraft).  Following push clearance; the tug began the push but we came to a stop after approx. 15 sec. I thought perhaps something crossed behind us and we would resume the push.  But; after a few more seconds; the tug driver said that a catering truck wasn't moving.  That seemed odd; and the Captain and I wondered why a catering truck wouldn't clear a moving aircraft.  That's when the Captain looked through his side window; over his shoulder and told me; 'THAT'S why the truck isn't moving - it's sitting under our wingtip!' We hadn't felt anything and the tug driver was asked if we were touching.  He said that he couldn't tell.  A crowd gathered.  I informed ramp of our situation and our intent to remain in position to investigate. A maintenance rep came on interphone and let us know it was difficult to determine how close the wingtip was to the roof of the truck.  It was judged safe to set brakes. After some time; it was decided to let air out of the truck's tires.  Personnel climbed atop the truck and after getting a closer look; the truck was moved.  No visible contact/damage was noted but the possibility was mentioned that the winds were moving the aircraft slightly and the wingtip may have bounced off the roof and that may have not been enough to show damage but that an inspection would be the best course of action.  We were cleared to be pulled forward to the gate and the aircraft was taken out of service and the crew and passengers deplaned to the aircraft at the adjoining gate.  The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Since we were being pushed straight back; we did not see the events leading up to the potential contact.  It would seem that a combination of catering truck driver and wing walker inattention may have contributed.[Suggest] Company communications to [the catering company] and maintenance re-iterating the need to be vigilant.
column123: About 60 feet into a routine pushback; the aircraft stopped.  The Tow Driver told us a 'catering truck driver is refusing to move.'  I asked if I should set the Parking Brake.  The Tow Driver said 'No.'  I looked out the left window and saw a catering truck with no driver in the cab.  I called Ramp Control on the radio to report the situation.     I looked out the window again to see a Maintenance Technician on the catering truck's over-the-cab loading platform.  He was leaning on the railing to look toward the aft-right side of the truck.  I opened the aircraft L2 Window to get a better view.  I saw the Left Wing apparently resting on the middle; top-right of the back portion of the catering truck.  I saw numerous Ground Crew and Maintenance personnel walking around the catering truck gesturing at the apparent contact point.     A Maintenance Supervisor saw me looking out the window and got on the Ground Interphone to tell me what was going on.  She said they thought there was actually no contact with the catering truck but couldn't be sure until they employed an operable hydraulic work lift - the first one they tried was inoperative.  I asked how big/small the gap was.  She thought the wing was about an inch from touching the truck; but the wind was causing the aircraft to gently rock; possibly bouncing the wing off the top of the truck.     After many minutes; a plan emerged to deflate the tires of the catering truck and tow it out of the way; preventing any possible further contact with the wing as the wind blew.  After the catering truck was clear; the Maintenance Supervisor got back on the Ground Interphone to tell us the aircraft was being taken out of service as a precaution and a replacement Ground Crew would tow us back to the gate for deplaning.  We were not to set the parking brake until safely at the gate.  Company Operations and Maintenance coordinated a different aircraft for us to continue the flight.     The tow was uneventful.  Once parked; we ran the Shutdown Checklist.  Maintenance Technicians boarded and asked us to not shut down the aircraft.  They also invited the First Officer and me to go outside and get on the work lift to inspect the wing.  To my eye; there was absolutely no indication of any kind that the wing had contacted the catering truck; however; I know that painted panels of modern materials can deform; return to shape; and not show outward signs of damage.  Not that it was my decision; but I concurred with Maintenance in taking the aircraft out of service.     Passengers and crew boarded the new aircraft and departed uneventfully.Cause Unknown.  I would only be speculating on events that occurred out of my view.I can only speculate how this event occurred; so I cannot provide prevention suggestions.

column121: Normal departure and flight enroute to ZZZ with thunderstorm approaching ZZZ airport on arrival from the west. Radar vectors for ILS XXL for approach; multiple speed adjustments from ATC on approach and no reports of wind gusts on initial arrival from ATC with winds 180/6 from ATIS. Storm had moved over field when on approach. On short final there was an RVR (Runway Visual Range) update from recall of greater than 5;000 RVR and moderate to heavy rain but no winds passed from recall. VMC around 1;100 feet and could see right and center runway but then went into torrential rain downpour around 400-500 feet on short final where Captain made an EFIS lights call and then I shortly after picked up runway lights and landing environment just prior to minimums and was a little high but was adjusting in close. Around 30-40 feet we had an instantaneous airspeed loss of around 10kts and at that time I had decided to go-around but with the airspeed loss and instantaneous loss of lift we touched down as go-around decision was made. We had a semi-hard landing and bounced and go-around selected all simultaneously. We were slow to put the speed brake back in after touching down but did eventually secure it and maintained attitude as we executed go around. Go-around procedures were completed airborne. Vectored back around by ATC for uneventful approach; landing and taxi in. The Captain and I both did a walk around of the aircraft post flight to ensure integrity of aircraft and check tail skid as a precaution but didn't notice the skid was ground down as we later were informed from the Director of Operations and Maintenance. We debriefed the event. Windshear/airspeed loss at low altitude while simultaneously executing go-around and didn't maintain proper go-around pitch once touching down as indicated from tail skid damage. Quicker reaction from crew with go-around with instantaneous airspeed loss and loss of lift and maintain proper attitude of aircraft on touchdown when executing go-around. Follow rules to live by; do not make large control inputs when in flare/go-around close to ground.
