column121: Climbing through 16;000 feet to FL 200 we experienced a high whistle sound from the front of the airplane. I felt pressure on my ears; nose; and head and had the air pushed out of my lungs. We identified a cabin depressurization and I reached for my O2 mask. I took a long inhale from the oxygen and then proceeded with additional memory items. The Captain began an priority descent. I reached for the Pax oxygen switch with my right hand and the PA button with my left hand. I communicated with the Captain that I was going off comms to tell Pax to put on oxygen masks. The Captain stated 'Wait. They are going to be fine here in 2-3 seconds and I don't want to replace the masks.' This occurred around 13;500 feet. So I did not complete memory items per the Captain's instruction. I contacted ATC and advised we were on an priority descent because of depressurization. We received a new assigned altitude of 10;000 feet. The Cabin started to repressurize around 11;000. ATC asked if we wished to declare priority handling and the Captain declined. We were able to continue to ZZZ without incident.There were several deviations from our normal operating procedures that concern me. First the disregard from memory items on the checklist. Second; the captain did not have his O2 mask plugged in. He believed he could plug it in fast enough if needed and that he doesn't plug it in because he forgets to unplug it after a flight. This caused a delay in performing a memory item. The Captain was able to plug his oxygen mask in but never donned it during controlled handling decent. Also; we did not formally ask for priority handling with ATC. We could not diagnose the problem for the rapid depressurization so we were unaware of what triggered it. I suggested declaring priority handling to cover our bases if anything else occurred. This flight had already been abnormal with the priority descent. The Captain disagreed saying the problem is over. Lastly; I do not believe the cockpit acceptance was completed for this flight. It is typical that the FO (First Officer) does the walk around and security check while the Captain is completing the acceptance. While doing the walk around it is very apparent that the shaker pusher test is being tested from outside the airplane. You can hear the shaking on the horizontal stabilizer. I did not hear it that morning. Also upon startup; the Captain found a popped circuit breaker on his side for De-Ice. I'm not sure when the circuit breaker popped but no de-icing equipment was on so I assume it was before startup. This is another missed item on the acceptance checklist. Now; these deviations did not cause the priority handling to occur but they could have added on to make the event worse.

column121: After the addition of thrust for T/O (takeoff) and selection of TO/GA (takeoff go-around) and N1 attaining T/O power; the aircraft was already rolling and had achieved approximately 15 knots of forward motion.  At that point we heard a very loud bang followed by a hard left yawing motion. The PF (Pilot Flying) immediately retarded the throttles to idle; and applied smooth breaking; which brought us to a complete stop.  We were angled left by about 30-40 degrees in relation to the center line of Runway 4; just prior to taxiway. I immediately informed ATC that we had stopped on the runway; the PF informed the PAX (passengers) to stay seated.  At that point we began to assess the situation. Initially we thought it was a blown tire or nose wheel steering issue. In that moment of assessing I noticed the #1 Engine Fail Caution illuminate in the #1 EGT Gauge. I informed the PF of the indication. It was the only indication we saw. No fire; no red lines only the engine failure alert caution. We reviewed the Rejected Takeoff Procedure; completed the QRH for Engine Failure. We then assessed the rolling and breaking capability of the aircraft and we found it to be normal.  We got clearance to exit the runway and return to the gate. As we pulled in to the gate; we remembered that we had not run an After Landing Checklist and quickly completed that; followed by the Parking Checklist. Then; the jetbridge malfunctioned and we had to wait until Airport Ops came to fix it. Once the jetbridge was attached I exited the aircraft to inspect Engine #1. I found the N1 fan blades and the stators directly behind them to be in a normal appearance. When I looked into the tailpipe of the turbine section; I found metal debris from the engine and both the aft fan blades and stators in front of them to be damaged and missing pieces. I hustled back to the Flight Deck to inform Ground Control that they needed to do a FOD check of the runway as we had; had and engine failure and that they needed to check for small engine parts.

column121: I was taking off on my 3rd and final takeoff and landing for my first solo. I had 3 great landings with my instructor and had landed twice solo and was going in for my final takeoff and landing. I was climbing in the pattern and was at 800 feet when I turned right over [road] then leveled the wings. Waited 3 seconds and turned parallel to the runway at 1;100 feet. Powered to 4500 RPM got the clearance to land from Tower and radioed back for clear to land. I pulled the carb heat and when I got to Â¾ of the runway I powered to 3000 RPM which is normal for a descent. I put in 2 seconds of flaps and took out the trim. I noticed I was a bit high at 900 feet when I turned over the shopping center so 100 feet above where I normally am. Put in some more flaps to about 20 degrees and turned in to final. I saw 3 whites and 1 red light; so I knew I was a bit high; I reduced power to get the plane to slow and reduce elevation. This gets me to the railroad tracks and descending in normally. Power is reduced to idle over the railroad tracks near Runway XX airplane starts to decent quicker than the last 2 times that I landed solo. As a result; I pitched up to get the glare shield on the horizon as that happened; I touched down and bounced on the runway. As the aircraft rose; I pitched for a decent angle thinking I was high above the runway; as the nose came over; I was surprised how close to the runway I was. Then I pitched for level flight; as I did this the aircraft touched down for a second; I thought It touched flat. But the nose dropped even more; this is when I heard the prop strike the runway. The aircraft went out of control veering to the left; as it departed the runway the nose gear collapses and digs into the dirt. The forward momentum of the airplane has the tail lifted off the ground before aggressively landing on the mains. the aircraft has come to a full stop; after stopping I paused for 3 seconds and then I contacted Tower and let them know what happened. After contacting Tower; I Opened my door and took off the seat belt; took the headset off and stepped out of the plan. I went out of the aircraft for 30 seconds before going back and turning the ignition off and turning off the master switch. After that I was met by airport ops.  After the initial shock and recuperating my thoughts I have found what mistakes I made on this solo and how this should have been avoided. Firstly; there is the initial bounce and when I caught air; I should have pushed into full power and pitched up to have the glare shield on the horizon which allows me to climb and then radio into Tower for a go-around. Definitely do not pitch down like I did and try to save the landing but rather go full power and pitch up for a climb. I was very appreciative of the airport ops and their quick action to make sure that I was safe and getting all the information to see how I didn't land correctly.

column121: I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg; approximately after 30 min of TOC; the lower display popped up showing Eng 2 low oil qty (3 qts); the Captain asked me to pull the QRH and look if there was a NNC (Non Normal Checklist); and we found out that there is no NNC for low oil quantity; upon searching our manuals we found information regarding this situation; explaining that there is not a min oil qty per se; but that oil temp and oil press are governing; and both indications we normal matching Eng 1. The Captain and I discussed the previous write up that the airplane had regarding low oil qty upon TOD; and how Maintenance personnel had previously drained the oil tank; filled it up again and checked for leaks. Since oil temperature and pressure indications were normal on Eng 2; we assumed it was an oil qty indication issue and decided to continue the flight closely monitoring Eng 2 oil temperature and pressure indications. In the following 10 to 15 mins the oil qty dropped to 0; but all other indications remained normal. Approximately 30 mins after the oil qty indication had shown 0 the Eng 2 oil pressure started to oscillate down and back up in a normal range; gradually getting lower every time; once it remained in the amber range the Captain and I started to anticipate a precautionary engine shutdown. Once the Eng 2 oil pressure indication entered the red range at approximately 14 PSI; the Captain called for the LOW OIL PRESS QRH NNC; we followed the NNC and proceeded to the ENG SHUTDOWN QRH NNC; we informed ATC and Dispatch of our mayday status and proceeded to ZZZ. After completing the ENG SHUTDOWN QRH; we proceeded to the ONE ENG INOPERATIVE NNC; dispatch sent us the landing data for ZZZ RWY XX We landed in ZZZ without further incident; stopping on the RWY and being towed to the ramp.The engine had developed an oil leak that went undetected.I understand the ZZZ1 Maintenance refilled the oil and perform an engine dry run; and then checked for leaks; perhaps the leak would have been discovered if the engine had been started and ran for several minutes.

column121: Upon landing on runway XX; we bounced slightly and then got hit by a gust from the left. As we re-contacted the ground; we were in a rightward drift and the learner failed to input a sufficient crosswind correction and I failed to call for a go-around. We slewed to the left into a ground loop causing minor scraping to the right wing tip.We taxied to the ramp and shut down and got out to inspect the airplane; finding minor skin damage to the right wing tip outboard of the aileron. We then decided to terminate the lesson.The learner (and airplane owner) had been off of flying for several weeks and had engaged me to help him get current again. We pre-briefed our plan of action and reviewed the weather and traffic conditions during an hour of ground school prior to starting up. The weather was good VFR with winds 270/9. I briefed that the forecast included a chance of winds gusting to 17 knots and that ZZZ might be busy on a nice Sunday afternoon. We took off and climbed up to 4;000' MSL and practiced some air work including engine failure turn back drills. We then entered the pattern at ZZZ Airport; to begin the pattern work. I was surprised that the pattern did not seem to be busy with only one other airplane in the pattern.  Everything had gone quite well until the gust caught us and I confess that I had begun to relax a bit too much and failed to call a go around after the bounce. As we finished up; I noted that the wind had shifted to 230/12G19; definitely over our stated max for the lesson. In retrospect; I should have been more assertive about not using the paved runway for the first few landings but should have suggested moving on to another airport with a good grass strip aligned with the wind. I should also have remained fully alert to the possibility of a poor first landing attempt.

column121: I took my third training flight in the twin engine aircraft with my instructor. After going missed from a circling approach to runway XX at ZZZ; the instructor simulated an engine failure by reducing the left throttle to idle. I went through the memory items for the engine failure after takeoff as I had practiced them in the simulator. With the single engine I climbed to 2000 feet and was vectored onto the ILS XX approach. Approaching minimums; my instructor told me to remove the view limiting device and I saw the runway. Shortly thereafter; he told me to go missed. I performed the missed approach flow but when I advanced the throttles; the airplane drifted to the left of the runway and did not climb. I had retracted the gear and flaps according to the procedure; but when we realized we were going to make contact with the ground; my instructor extended the landing gear. We bounced once and the second time we contacted the ground; we veered to the left and came to a stop. Loss of power in the left engine at low altitude
column123: During my third training flight in the light twin aircraft; we performed the LOC XX approach into ZZZ; concluding with a circle to runway XX1. We went missed from runway XX1 and flew straight out. During the climb; the instructor simulated an engine failure by retarding the left throttle to idle. I performed all the memory items as I had practiced them in the simulator: while maintaining directional control and airspeed; I smoothly moved the mixtures; then props; then throttles to the full forward position; and then when I had determined that the left engine was the failed one; I placed the left fuel pump forward to the high position. The left throttle was at idle. Then I reached for the left engine mixture control. I expected my instructor's hand to be blocking the quadrant but it wasn't. I checked with him and he told me to continue with the procedure. I reduced the left mixture to idle after which he pushed the control forward slightly. I reduced the left prop to feather and then he pushed this forward slightly as well. After the memory items; I pulled out the QRH to complete the procedure. During this time ZZZ tower switched us over to approach and we requested the ILS XX. My instructor was on the radios. When I opened the QRH; he told me to turn the autopilot on; which I did. After that; I completed the engine failure flow according to the QRH; except that I only touched and verbalized the items relating to the left engine; and did not move any switches. We were vectored for the ILS XX approach and I ran the in-range and before landing checklists according to the QRH. On final approach; my instructor had brought the left engine mixtures and props full forward. Just before minimums; he told me to look up and I saw the runway in front of me. The PAPIs indicated that I was on glidepath and we were set up for a landing in the touchdown zone. He told me to go around. I pressed the mixture controls forward (they were already full forward); then the propeller controls (already full forward); then throttles full forward; and began to apply back pressure and as I did so. I noticed the airplane did not respond as it had during the previous go-around. The airplane was drifting to the left of the runway center line. I retracted the flaps. Then I retracted the landing gear. All of this happened within a matter of seconds. The airplane was significantly left of center line; flying over the grass. I tried to use the aileron and rudders to fly a straight course. It was not climbing at the rate I expected. I scanned the controls and instruments to see what could be the matter. Everything seemed to be in place. I noticed the airspeed was low-- around 80 knots-- and I released back pressure to prevent a stall. At this point I realized that my instructor was speaking loudly and with urgency about the landing gear. I had just retracted the landing gear. Thinking that he wanted to reduce drag for the climb; I told him 'landing gear is retracted.' He reached across the cockpit and placed the gear in the down position. It was at this point that I realized that he wanted the gear down because we were going to make contact with the ground. Within seconds of him placing the gear in the down position; we did make contact with the ground. I believe he and I both were at the controls at this point. We contacted the ground hard once; bounced slightly; then contacted the ground again; at which point the airplane veered to the left and came to a stop.My instructor contacted tower and told them that there were no injuries. Tower said emergency vehicles were on their way. I motioned to the switches and asked 'should we turn them off?' He said 'yes-- battery and alternators [motioning with his hand] and magnetos.' I turned these off; then the pump switches. I then looked out the window and surveyed the damage. I saw the tip of the left wing in contact with the ground; the bent props of the left engine; and the long groove in the turf created by thedragging left wheel. Then emergency personnel arrived and we exited the airplane.I saw the left fuel pump on high after the airplane came to a stop. I think the fuel pump being left on high flooded the engine; preventing it from supplying power during the go-around. Prior to this flight I had done a couple of simulator sessions involving an engine failure; and I had witnessed several simulator sessions which involved engine failures. During all of these sessions; the fuel pump on the faulty or inoperative engine was brought to high. During one simulator session; the instructor made a point of showing that this could solve the issue.I do not remember being told that during an actual training flight in the airplane; the pump should not be turned to high. During the previous training flight; I was told that on the inoperative engine I should only 'touch and tell' and not flip switches. I remembered this and did not flip any switches dealing with the left engine during my flight; which meant that I kept the left fuel pump on high.1. Make it more clear in training that the fuel pump being turned to high can cause the engine to flood and fail to restart. 2. Before doing a simulated engine failure in flight; make it more clear that the fuel pump being turned to high is the one memory item that ought to be simulated... or; that instead of 'touch and tell' on all the items related to the failed engine; it should be 'touch and tell on all items except the fuel pump; which should be turned to the off position'

column121: A student of mine and I were conducting performance landings and traffic pattern operations at ZZZ. On our second lap in the pattern I instructed my student to conduct a short field landing to a full stop. In the downwind my student made a comment about using maximum braking and how it would wear the brakes easily. I instructed the student to verbalize 'simulated' maximum braking to prevent wear on the aircraft braking system. On short final everything was looking great; the main gear touched down on the 1000 foot markers softly. My student then locked the right main brake; causing the right tire to skid. I announced 'off the brakes' to allow the aircraft to roll. My student let off the right brake and then began locking the left brake; causing the left brake to lock inducing a tire skid. I announced 'off the brakes' again multiple times; and the student did not let off the brakes. At this time I announced 'my controls' to take control of the airplane; multiple times; again the student did not come off any flight controls. During this time of trying to regain control of the aircraft from my student; the left main tire blew; causing the wheel pant to crush due to the flat tire and rubber off the tire. The aircraft rolled to a stop on the runway approximately 30 feet off center-line with 20 feet to the left edge. At this time with the aircraft at a complete stop; I called on CTAF for ZZZ to let other aircraft know we were disabled on the runway; unable to taxi due to the left main tire being flat. At this time we left power to the aircraft to allow usage of the radios to monitor while my rear seated passenger (a student observing our lesson) made a call to the local FBO to request a tow. The workers at the FBO NOTAM'ed the runway closed for 1 hour to allow safe removal of the aircraft from the runway environment. The aircraft was removed from the runway in approximately 25 minutes by using a dolly under the left main.

column121: During walk-around; [the] FO (First Officer) found a dent in [the] aircraft; aft left side; near lavatory service. [The case was] entered into [the] AML and [we] informed Maintenance. Contract Maintenance took pictures; detailed measurements; and notes for submittal to ZZZ2 Maintenance Control. After approximately an hour; it was determined that [the] aircraft was good to go; item was deferred; and the paperwork was completed. Flight was uneventful to ZZZ1. At the gate in ZZZ1; a Mechanic came out to the aircraft with some ACARS paper that was requested inbound. We mentioned the dent; so he said he would go take a look. During this time; [the] aircraft was serviced; passengers were boarded; and the flight was 'ready' for departure. The door was actually closed when the Crew Chief informed us that we were on a maintenance hold. The same Mechanic returned and told us that the dent was very significant and the aircraft should be taken out of service for repairs. He mentioned that the aircraft shouldn't have flown and was a 'blowout' waiting to happen. A Maintenance Supervisor came out; evaluated the situation; and the aircraft was subsequently taken out of service. Why and how was it determined that the aircraft was 'good to go' at an outstation; but when the plane gets to a hub it's taken out of service? I understand a forward-leaning mentality when it comes to serving our passengers but this should never be at the expense of safety. We were informed by the Maintenance Supervisor that the discrepancy was deferred in ZZZ but the aircraft was to undergo further evaluation when it arrived in ZZZ1. This sounds plausible; except; the only reason the discrepancy was 'further evaluated' was because we needed ACARS paper and happened to mention the dent to an experienced and highly trained Mechanic; who applied the brakes to this situation. Mistakes can happen; but in situations where there is doubt regarding airworthiness; it is better to err on the side of caution.

column121: At initial entry into the flight deck; a large amount of coffee was spilled on the aft; center; pedestal of our Airbus A319. Despite an immediate clean up with a large number of paper towels; the first noted impact may have been the failure of the ACARS printer; as indicated by an MCDU message; and the failure of the 'Slew' button to advance any paper. We then began a long series of phone calls with our dispatcher and Maintenance Control (conferenced in) to both attempt a reset of the printer or secure an MEL entry. The total time on the phone was likely over 30 minutes; after which we had an ACARS printer MEL. During our extensive time on hold; I began to suspect that some of the coffee may have also entered other components; such as the Flap/Slat and Spoiler control modules; all near the ACARS printer. After advising Maintenance Control of this; their guidance was to cycle the various components at the gate to see if they worked; we did so; but that generated a FLT/C ECAM Slat Sys error message. Maintenance Control suggested that we try the tests again; once both engines were running; which we did. Both systems appeared to operate nominally so we dismissed our push crew for taxi out. Within 2 to 4 minutes of commencing taxi; I noted an electrical odor; followed soon thereafter by visible whiffs of electrical smoke coming from the ACARS printer area. I directed the First Officer to immediately pulled the ACARS printer Circuit Breaker (as we knew from our earlier Maintenance Control-directed troubleshooting); but found it had already popped. We returned to the gate after consulting with Maintenance Control and local operations; whereupon our aircraft was eventually removed from service.This was arguably the greatest failure of my entire aviation career; I am aghast that we allowed this situation to progress as far is it did; particularly in light of the 'What If's?' We almost took off in an aircraft with grossly uncertain airworthiness. An after-the-fact Google search reveals a long history of potentially catastrophic aviation emergencies and incidents from cockpit fluid spills; we would have added to this list if the ACARS printer had happened to begin smoking a few minutes later; or if the spoilers or flaps/slats had had an uncommanded movement; or if the Engine Master Control(s) had detected a false 'Off' signal...all from a stray drop of coffee migrating to the wrong place at the worst time.While there are many parties to this series of mistakes; I feel that Maintenance Control guidance in this matter was woefully incorrect and caused a serious; negative; impact on our flight's safety. Furthermore; our own flight training has been deficient; we should have known to ground the aircraft. Had we been correctly trained on this threat; we would have never left the gate. Prior to this event; I had little understanding of the potential damage from fluid spills; now I know better; particularly after seeing the coffee stains near the cannon plugs and wiring of essential items inside the center pedestal. Lastly; we were not the first; nor will we be the last; to spill something on the flight deck: the FAA and other aviation authorities should quickly establish Technical Standard Orders for all equipment in 'spill zones' so as to prevent potentially catastrophic outcomes going forward.

column121: I was parked on the gravel bar with the tail of the plane oriented significantly downhill. I had the parking brake set but also used a good size piece of driftwood to chock the left main tire. When it was time to leave; I released the parking brake while still outside the aircraft; which is the only practical way to release it since the lever is situated deep within the footwell. However; when I removed the log (so as not to hit it with my tailwheel when taxiing) the plane started to roll. Therefore I reset the parking brake; deciding to release it from inside the cockpit after starting the engine to provide enough thrust from rolling backward while I reached within the footwell to release the parking brake lever. I struggled slightly but was able to reach the parking brake lever and satisfied it was released I increased power and the plane began to move forward. Taxiing was sluggish but this was expected due to the low-inflation bush tires combined with two other factors: the 'digging' or plowing of the tailwheel and the soft gravel/sand. The tail wheels of all aircraft were digging that day; causing extra power to be needed for ground operations. We deal with this situation every time we land and takeoff from gravel bars and had dealt with it the previous 10 takeoffs and landings earlier this day. So at the time I didn't notice or feel anything unexpected during taxi.As I lined up for takeoff; I took notice of the same small bush I always use on this gravel bar as an abort point if my tail isn't up and flying as well as a familiar tree I use as my abort point if I am not airborne by the time I reach it. I applied full power and well before the small bush abort-point; my tail was already up and flying. This was unusual as it normally takes much longer for the tail to come up but I mistakenly saw this as a good thing so I continued the takeoff roll. A second or two later; I was suspicious that I wasn't accelerating normally so began preparing to abort if not airborne by my second abort point. I momentarily diverted my eyes from outside the cockpit to check my airspeed and this check confirmed my suspicions - I was not accelerating normally. As I began to pull the throttle off; I hit a small rut and momentarily became airborne a few inches so I hesitated a fraction of a second to abort the takeoff. However; I settled back to the surface and instantly; before I had a chance to pull the throttle to idle; it felt as if the tires 'grabbed' and the resulting inertia put the plane on its nose and the remaining momentum caused it to flip over onto its back. I was able to exit the aircraft quickly and within seconds; several people were there to assist me. Multiple people then assisted me with carefully turning the plan back over and we were all very surprised at the lack of damage. Other than the propeller; some scrapes and scratches to the paint and a crack in the top of the [type] windscreen; there were no other obvious signs of damage. We pushed the plane out of the way and secured it and I was given a ride with one of my friends to ZZZ1 where we spent the night as planned.Unable to figure out what happened I began recreating the events that led up to the incident and became suspicious that even though I was able to taxi; maybe I had not fully released the parking brake. Returning to the plane the next day; I opened the door and several of us looked inside and saw the position of the parking brake lever. It was barely to the halfway position. I'm not familiar enough with the internal valving to know for sure; but the halfway-released parking brake lever seemed to confirm my theory. The chain of events leading up to this incident were extremely interesting and like any error chain; there were numerous opportunities to break it; beginning from the moment I landed on the gravel bar and picked my parking spot.  I only parked my plane in the same manner because everyone else was parked that way. However; I could have simply chosen to park farther away from the bank on more level ground; thus avoiding the need to use the parking brake to begin with. The next opportunity came when I first removed the log and the plane began rolling backwards. I could have simply asked any one of 10 people to help me keep the plane from rolling while I released the parking brake (from outside the cockpit as I always have in the past) thus enabling me to get in and start the engine. The next opportunity to break the error chain came when I accepted the sluggish taxi as 'normal' thus exhibiting confirmation bias. Rather than being more suspicious I was actually being complacent. Yet another chance to break the error chain was when my tailwheel came up unusually quickly. Had I recognized this situation as abnormal (rather than welcoming the unusual 'bonus' of the tail coming up so quickly) I could've accomplished an easy; low speed abort and checked everything to see what was amiss. Finally; the last chance I had to avoid this outcome was to abort as soon as I became suspicious of my lack of acceleration rather than focusing on my predetermined abort point. Once I went beyond that last opportunity to abort; I believe my fate was pretty much sealed. Contributing factors (in my opinion) were an unusually large 'audience' of fellow pilots watching our group of planes takeoff. This probably reveals the biggest failing on my part that day. Ego. Not wanting to screw up in front of a bunch of fellow pilots. Looking back; a simple aborted takeoff would never have been seen as a screw up but the exact opposite. Everyone on that gravel bar would've been extremely supportive of the prudent decision to abort. For ANY reason whatsoever. Maybe another contributing factor could be the design/location of the parking brake lever of the [Homebuilt type]. Though I hesitate to include this as a factor as the location of the parking brake lever had never been an issue in the past. But this unusual scenario may have shined some light on a potentially troubling aspect of the location of the parking brake lever deep within the footwell as opposed to someplace in plain sight and easy to manipulate and confirm whether it is set or released. All in all; this was a scenario fraught with poor aeronautical decision making and will inform my attitude towards flying for the rest of my time spent piloting aircraft; regardless of which type of aircraft I am flying. Lessons learned.

column121: On Date there was an unfortunate damage to the Right Horizontal Stabilizer of Aircraft X. This damage drove Safety Bulletin on Date 1; which suggested a breakdown in communication as the root cause of the damage. However; most technicians (and supervisors) believe the real root cause of this damage was caused by the inability to use the correct equipment to accomplish the task at hand due to [the] Stores Department using both sides of this bay as staging and storage for their various equipment and items (tires; crates of all types and sizes; stacked at heights of over 10 feet in some instances). The work to be accomplished was on the right hand wing tip but because of all the equipment on the ground a small 35 feet JLG or widebody lift could not be used; instead a much larger JLG was necessary; positioned much further away; resulting in contact/damage to the right horizontal stabilizer. If this was a one off; the technicians probably would not have as much heartburn but this issue of stores using Bay 3; one of our prime widebody aircraft bays; as a storage has been going on for years and has resulted in other aircraft damages in the past.  This has been a well-documented and hot topic of discussion in ZZZ meetings; crew briefings; safety team raising it with messages; every level of management has been made aware of this over the years.  Sadly; the situation is getting worse instead of better.At our latest ZZZ meeting Date 1; a supervisor questioned the findings of the investigation stating that in his experience working the service center; he felt the stores equipment was more of a causation factor than the loss of communication. The reply from another member of management 'I am not aware of this being an issue'. Another participant suggested there was a lot of documentation but was told 'we can look into it and maybe build a case to get the stores equipment moved'. Since the damage; this stores equipment problem has been highlighted at the daily crew briefings and what is glaring to most techs since this damage is the fact that not only has nothing been done to mitigate the issue; it has actually gotten worse since the latest damage. This aircraft has been out of service now for almost 3 weeks; (if we are to believe the finance people when they tell us that a wide body generates X money on average a day); that's a costly stores area; just looking at it from that perspective!The unfortunate reality is in the event of a damage the technician is grilled in the investigation; sent for drug and alcohol testing; always made to feel at fault; always told it was self-induced pressure; and of course have their records pulled showing they signed off a specific training course; maintenance & engineering bulletin; awareness class etc. I have examples of this from many investigation reports.  I'm filing this report because the front-line mechanics don't want to for fear of repercussions if they did.  Sure; there are many human factors that come into play when incidents like this happen but when you look at it; this is not complacency on the part of the mechanics. There are real pressures to get these aircraft in and worked in BAY 3 and we crutch the system on a daily basis because of these pressures.  My question; how is Company living up to their values of safety always being #1 when this issue has been ignored for years despite the attention and spotlight?What is staggering to most; weeks after the latest very costly damage the situation is actually worse. The only answer could be; if you investigate and find the root cause that suits; then of course it will be impossible to mitigate and address the real root cause! I won't gain any friends for pointing this out but this issue needs to be addressed. It is our responsibility; from safety; to Management; coworkers etc.; to do the right thing; provide a safe work environment; which helps keep us all safe from injury and our assets from being damaged. We owe it to each other and ourcustomers. At this juncture this needs to be a priority from senior leadership because constant suggestions and concern from the floor have hit a brick wall and frankly we on the front line don't have the authority to fix the problem.

column121: Prior to making the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; I met with my Flight Instructor to review my flight plan and briefing which I created. All parameters were within the confines of my limitations for my student pilot endorsements for a student solo; cross-country operation. This was my first cross-county solo flight in the aircraft. I was to make two full-stop landings at ZZZ1 as part of the flight; then return to ZZZ. Takeoff from ZZZ and cruise to ZZZ1 were uneventful. I flew at 5;500 feet and reported transitioning the airspace above a non-controlled airport along the way. Immediately after reporting this transition; and well prior to entering the Delta Airspace of ZZZ1; I switched my COM2 radio to ZZZ1 and got the latest automated weather report. I do not recall what the letter designation for the report was at the time; but the weather was clear with good visibility of 10+ miles; winds relatively calm; and a clear sky. I then radioed the tower at ZZZ1 on their frequency and identified myself as a student pilot solo flight along with my relative position west of the airport and requested a full-stop landing while approximately 15nm away.The Tower answered saying they were having difficulty hearing my transmission and to restate my position. I spoke more loudly and clearly; identifying my position as west at about 14.6 miles. They advised me to re-contact them when less than a mile from the runway.  I began a descent appropriate to arrive at pattern altitude prior to radio contact. When I got within a mile I radioed the tower and the tower advised me to turn for my base and that I was cleared to land. I executed turns to base and final without issue and extended full flaps incrementally. Upon entering final approach with full-flaps I was just high of the glideslope as indicated by the PAPI system. I entered my flair and 'ballooned' slightly. When I came back down from ballooning; I came down hard and in the process; experienced prop strike; front gear collapse; and damage to my right wing before coming to a stop on the grass to the left of the runway with the help of the grass to arrest my momentum. The plane came to rest in a nose-down fashion at an approximate 45 degree angle to the edge of the runway and in the direction of the landing. After announcing over the radio that they have a crash on the runway; the tower radioed me to ask my condition and I replied that I was fine. I then noticed fuel leaking from my right wing and elected to shut down electrical items as a precaution. When the airport firetruck arrived; the operator sprayed foam on the area leaking as a precaution for the fuel leak. After several minutes; the responding airport staff strapped the nose wheel to the fuselage and were able to pull the plane to a storage hangar with a tractor by keeping the plane on the main landing gear and tugging the plane via the tail tie-down.

column121: Pushed back from the ZZZ gate X; during push back; we received the okay from ground crew personnel that we can start engine 1. During engine start of the number one engine; it was noted that we had a hung start as the N2 gauge only got up to about 31 percent. Once the Captain and I noticed the indications; we went into shutdown procedures of the number 1 engine. We did note the engine 1 ITT temperature rapidly increase; before it decreased. After shutting down the engine to prepare to restart; ground crew personnel attempted to notify us that there was a fire. However; due to faulty headsets of ground personnel; this information was hard to make sense of. At this point to confirm a potential fire; we contacted the flight attendants to check the rear of the aircraft and look out the windows to confirm the fire potential. The flight attendants did not see any flames or smoke. The decision was made to open the main cabin door; to allow the pilot in command to visually verify there was a fire threat. After the pilot in command visually inspected the area; he was able to confirm that there was a fire and we promptly called for an aircraft evacuation of the passengers and crew. Fire units were notified promptly by ground crew and notification to ZZZ Ground Control of evacuation of passengers on the ramp. The Captain and myself (First Officer) continued to do the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist and the Passenger Evacuation Procedure Checklist.
column123: Pushing back we were cleared to start the number one engine. While starting the engine we noticed the engine went to 30 percent N2 and N1 was hanging at 6 to 7 percent. When we were doing the shutdown procedure we noticed the ITT gauge started going up rapidly then went down to zero after we shut down the engine and had no other messages appear on the aircraft. After we shut down the engine the rampers were trying to tell us something; but their radio had a lot of static and I could not understand them. I thought they said fire; but I was not sure because of all the static on the radio. We had no indication on the EICAS of an engine fire. I had my First Officer call the Flight Attendant and check to see if there was a fire. They called back and said they could not see anything. Still unable to understand what ramp was saying; I decided to open the cabin door to visually check; and there was a fire on the number 1 engine. I ran back inside and told the Flight Attendants to evacuate the aircraft. The First Officer and I ran the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist. After we finished the checklist I shut off the aircraft and made sure everyone was off the aircraft.

column121: I departed with one passenger to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful until on a 5-mile final when I heard the Tower clear a 'Heavy' cargo plane to take the runway for departure. As we got closer to the runway; we noticed that the heavy cargo plane was just getting off the runway as we were on short final. With traffic behind us in the pattern; I continued the approach opting to land slightly below the glideslope on the first third of the runway so as to avoid any potential wake turbulence put off by the departing aircraft beyond its rotation point. While in the landing phase of flight; approximately 1' off the ground and near stall speed for a normal landing; we encountered sudden turbulence that caused the plane to destabilize resulting in a brief touchdown followed by a balloon and a subsequent stall that caused the aircraft to bounce on the runway. As I saw we were losing directional control; I added full power to initiate the go-around maneuver; regained stability; and completed a left traffic pattern. We came in shortly after another Cirrus on short final and had a normal smooth landing. It was not until after taxiing to [FBO] and performing engine shutdown that I noticed the tips of the props were frayed as the obvious result of a prop strike on our initial attempt.It is my opinion that the cause of the turbulence encountered on the runway was the jet blast from the departing heavy jet rather than wake turbulence as we landed well before its point of rotation. While I do not have a copy of the Tower's audio; I do not recall any warnings from the Tower. Apparently; the 'heavy' jet took an extended amount of time to take the runway after being cleared and departed less than a minute before our touchdown. Since we could not see the plane delay taking the runway from a distance due to haze; the Tower should have warned us to avoid wake turbulence and jet blast during our approach. This would likely have prompted a decision to break off our approach at a safe altitude to allow the jet blast to dissipate; and follow trailing traffic to an uneventful landing.At 120 kts. approach speed; our ETA to land on a 5-mile final was approximately 2.5 minutes. Had the Tower held the 'heavy' cargo jet for the additional few minutes; substantial loss of property and the potential for loss of life could have been avoided. In hindsight; as PIC I could have made the decision to break off on short-final and abort the landing when I noticed the heavy cargo plane had departed so shortly before we were to land. I trusted the Tower to provide safe and adequate separation for our arrival and it could have cost us a lot more than a prop strike. I will not make that mistake again.

column121: Aircraft was directed to taxi from gate 1 to Runway XXL via Taxiways 1; 2; 3; 4. While on Taxiway 3; turning right to join Taxiway 4; both crew members noted an aircraft that appeared to have just been pushed back from gate 2. It was also agreed by both crew members that the tail of the aircraft appeared to be just inside the ramp boundary line. Approaching the aircraft at gate 2; the FO noted that the right wingtip was on the boundary line. The Captain then stated that he was going to deviate left of the taxiway centerline for additional clearance and the FO acknowledged. Approaching the aircraft; the FO was monitoring the right wingtip. From the cockpit angle the wingtip appeared to have approximately five feet of clearance and this was communicated to the Captain. The FO continued to monitor the wingtip until it appeared to initially pass the tail of the other aircraft outside of gate 2 and then announced it was clear to the Captain. It was at this time the right winglet struck the horizontal stabilizer. (Aircraft  speed was approximately 5 knots.)  The FO then called out to stop multiple times. The Captain stopped the aircraft and made an announcement for the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain in their seats. The Captain verified with the Flight Attendants that everyone was OK. The crew then coordinated with Ground Control and Operations to return to gate 3. An ACARS message was also sent to Dispatch while waiting for a gate assignment. It is the FO's initial assessment that the wingtip must have started to pass on the opposite side of the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft outside of gate 2; but incorrectly determined that it was on the near side based off the cockpit angle and understanding that the Captain had deviated left of the taxiway for more clearance. There were no distractions and the crew communicated clearly.  Actions that could have prevented this incident would have been if the crew had stopped on Taxiway 4 and waited for the aircraft at gate 2 to move and provide more clearance. Additionally; the FO could have better assessed the wingtip spacing.
column123: We were cleared to taxi from [gate] 1 to [Runway] XXL via [taxiways] 2; 3 and 4. As we were joining 4; I noticed an aircraft facing terminal at [gate] 2; which appeared to be just inside of the movement area line. I mistakenly assumed it was an aircraft that had just pushed and that he was waiting to taxi. My expectation bias was that he would not have been pushed deep enough to interfere with Taxiway 4. As we were NE bound on [Taxiway] 4; I steered aircraft left of taxi; centerline to give more clearance around other aircraft. I asked FO how we looked on wingtip clearance. The FO stated; 'We are clear by 5 to 10 feet.' As we were passing behind the aircraft I felt that a main tire hit a pothole. As I asked what that was; I felt another 'bump'. The FO stated 'Stop. Stop.' I brought the aircraft to a stop and the FO told me we struck the other aircraft. I would estimate we were at a speed of 7 to 8 knots when the contact occurred. We began our taxi on #2 engine. I believe the second engine start was complete prior to contact. There was a typical level of chatter on ZZZ Ground frequency; which was busy. After the contact; I stopped the aircraft on Taxiway 4 and set the parking brake. We reported the incident to Ground Control. While I made a PA to the cabin to remain seated; the FO notified operations to coordinate a gate return and contact Maintenance. We returned to Gate 3 without further incident.Task Loading - I did a poor job of managing task loading. ZZZ is very busy and congested on the ground. With multiple aircraft moving in a densely packed area; I should not have opted for Single Engine Taxi (SET).  This would have reduced the workload on both crew members and perhaps allowed for better situational awareness as we were moving towards the departure runway. Risk Management- I did not properly balance the risk of aircraft contact with continuing on the taxiway. Had I stopped and waited on the other aircraft to move well clear of taxiway; I would not have assumed that unnecessary risk. This also relates to rushing and trying not to clog up a taxiway. I should have set the brakes and not moved forward until aircraft in question was well clear.

column121: I'm writing because I have concern over the quality of the DJI Mavic Air 2.  During my post flight inspection of my drone; I noticed fatigue cracking in the body of the UAV.  The cracking is right around the pilot point for the front motor supports.  I've done some research online and noticed that this apparently is a common problem among other DJI Mavic Air 2 operators.  I did some digging and I noticed that the FAA currently doesn't regulate small UAVs; and I have concerns over the process to close any safety concerns with these manufacturers.  There seems to be a gap as the FAA really would like to regulate the operations of the vehicle; but they currently don't have standards in place for the certification of the vehicles.  From my perspective there needs to be some sort of regulations in place to ensure the UAVs will operate safely and the burden of airworthiness should not be bore solely by the operator; but OEMs need to take responsibility for their equipment as well.  Note; that I did land without any incident; and have reached out to DJI on the matter and I will not be flying until the issue is resolved.

And eventually received a call from the Chief Pilot confirming that there was damage to main landing gear and he wanted to hear from me what had happened. I explained to the Chief Pilot what had happened; and Chief Pilot took notes and said to follow up with an Ops report.A firmer landing than normal due to minimal flare that caused the main landing gears to come into contact with the runway quicker than normal due to minimal flare. FO barely flared during a visual approach at Runway XXL in ZZZ that ended up causing a hard landing situation.[Reporter recommends] possibly rotate brand new FO's and make them fly more often. [The maintenance airport] experienced heavy rainfall for an extended period prior to flight. Flight was uneventful until the descent phase of flight. At approximately FL220; the radar showed 'Weather (WX) FAIL' accompanied by a grinding noise; as if the radar was stuck on one side of the sweep. Radar was secured. At approximately 15;000 MSL and 325 knots in the descent; an additional loud bang and excessive airflow noise occurred; accompanied by multiple EICAS messages; including 'IAS DISAGREE.' Captain's side display was showing approximately 250 knots. F/O's side display was showing approximately 330 knots; which agreed with standby instrumentation. F/O called for 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. The autopilot and autothrottles (A/T) were disengaged; and the A/T ARM switch was turned off. F/O continued flying manually throughout the remainder of the flight. Captain elected to leave the Flight Directors on; as the lateral guidance was still valid; we were VMC; and at that range we already had the field in sight. It was agreed that the F/O would disregard the pitch guidance until the instrumentation issue could be corrected. Captain continued running through the checklist from the QRH; it was determined that the F/O's instrumentation was valid; and the Captain selected the right side Air Data Compute (ADC). From that point forward; as we slowed to 250 knots; the airplane essentially flew normally. F/O continued to manually hand fly the descent and approach to an uneventful landing. After inspection; the aircraft was taxied back normally. On post-flight inspection; the radome had a large structural failure; which likely caused an asymmetric airflow disruption which affected the Captain's instrumentation.

column121: I; RPIC; was tasked with conducting cell tower inspections in the greater pacific northwest area for the drone company. I was using a drone that had known issues with camera gimbal yet with no other options or support from the company; I had to continue to fly with this drone. This drone was known for its gimbal locking and or becoming unresponsive to the drone's heading when flown. Problems with this drone were brought to my attention by my flight trainer prior to me taking over the drone; and I had also informed my mission coordinator of the problems with the gimbal after I had taken over the drone to continue the operation. Upon take off; I encountered the gimbal lock again. Before I could land and calibrate the gimbal; a substantial gust overcame my area of operation from the West/Southwest. As a reactionary response; I pushed the right stick forward (into the Southern Direction) to send the drone away from the traffic behind me; to the North. The gusts appeared to be above the operational limits of the drone and I adjusted the right and left stick to aim into the wind. I looked back up in the air to find the drone to evaluate if it was safe to do an emergency landing into the grand land; or to find a safe descend path. With the gimbal unresponsive to the drone's heading; I was unable to correctly judge the drone's flight path which was directly into an oncoming tree. This tree was outside my operational area; and therefore was above my MOCA (Minimum Obstacle Clearance Avoidance). It was not my intent to fly beyond my operational area; but as an inadvertent contingency for safety of those on the road; the safest area for an emergency landing was beyond the grounds of the tower. My thought was that the grass seed would have been a suitable/softer area to land; versus the hard gravel of the maintenance road; or induce the hazardous possibility of a highway incursion with highway traffic. The justification for my flight response is that by flying towards the grass seed land; I would have absolutely mitigated the risk of causing serious injury or death; and or substantial damage by causing an aviation accident with the highway or any case that could have been defined by the 49 CFR 830. By the time I reacted to the tree being in frame of my camera; my counter maneuvers did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The anti-collision sensors of the drone also did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The drone has and always was in Position Hold mode and was not deviated from. Even with the wind gusts pushing the drone to its limit; the anti-collision sensors should have detected the tree and stopped the aircraft from colliding with the tree or at least assisted my counter maneuvers in preventing the accident. In response to the weather; my anemometer was reading 2-9 mph on the ground. This wave of gusts was unexpected and arbitrary to the regular wind speeds I had been enduring for the entire site audit. To the Southwest; I did notice very dark cumulonimbus clouds which may have been a severe thunderstorm forming; which may have caused instability upwind. I was able to find the drone near the tree in the grass seed bush. The camera has completely broken off; the landing gear had sustained fractures; the main profile has been disconnected; and one propeller was broken. This drone is not safe to fly in its current state and will need repair from manufacturer. In this flyaway accident; there was no serious injury; death; or substantial damage that occurred beyond the aircraft and the surrounding environment. I wanted to bring this accident to light because of the post crash situation. The drone was lost in grass seed bushes that were at least 4-5ft tall. I had to walk through the bush with my best guesses to where the drone was actually at. Since the drone battery had disconnected with the drone; I was not able to use the GPS homing software on the tablet to find where the drone was. After some timesearching; I eventually found the drone and the camera. But I have yet to find the battery. From my understanding of the DJI drones; if the battery is disconnected while it is in the 'on' mode; the battery will continue to discharge. After some time; the LiPO battery will eventual become depleted and not pose as a threat to the grass seed bushes. However; in any case that the battery should still pose a threat to the grass seed bushes; I think a contingency should be put in place with modern commercial drones that would benefit and promote safety in post crash events. My thought is that audible micro speakers could be places with the intelligent flight batteries that will sound an alarm if the battery is armed and not in a fixed / connected position with the aircraft. It is the same principles as black boxes for manned aviation. In this scenario; this battery is lost in some field of very high and very dense bush that does not allow me to find the battery without extra aid from more people; metal detectors; or other mechanical means of detection. But; that some chime or sound be presented by an improperly disengaged 'on' battery; I would have been able to find and locate nearly all components of the air craft swiftly and with haste. The fact that even with me scanning a 50ft radius of the crash site and I could not find the most critical and unsafe component to the drone raises the question of 'how can we improve post commercial drone crashes.' I think by having some alarm attached to the battery would aid in the post crash finding time and recovery. Even with the battery discharged; it may still pose a threat to the field; making it unsafe for its presence to be there. In theory; by attaching a speaker to the battery; you would add a safety system as another line of defense in protecting the crash scene environment from future substantial damages.  Contributing factors are company's lack of critical response for repairs or replacements of a commercial aircraft; extreme weather phenomena changes; hardware failure in the anti collision sensors; and hardware failure in the main visual optical sensor.

column121: ZZZ MX (Maintenance) called and informed that the LH eng took 19 Quarts. MX inspected the inside and outside of the eng cowl and eng; tailpipe; inlet and behind fan blades with no evidence of a leak. The inbound crew did not write up a problem with the oil QTY. We reviewed AHM (Automated Health Monitoring) report with was posted inflight an hour prior to landing and showed good QTY and oil pressure and no high oil temp. We reviewed the oil service screen in work bench and no servicing has been done for a while which showed no oil consumption issues. We asked to MX service the oil tank and run the engine; no leaks found and a good oil gulp at start which tells us the tank is not over serviced. We put the engine oil qty on MEL for two reasons one that the oil qty transmitter was giving false readings and MX may have thought when they checked the gauge in the cockpit that the engine was full and that's why the oil screen also showed very little oil servicing of the engine. Second reason is that by putting the engine on MEL that forces the mechanic to check oil at the tank and document it. There for showing if we truly have an oil consumption problem. We monitored the take off and looked at the takeoff report and it showed good oil qty and pressure. About an hour later we got a report of the engine having high oil temp. We looked at AHM; it did show a high oil temp with oil Qty and pressure good. On post landing at ZZZ1 MX did a look at the engine and once again no leaks found. With the oil temp high that's when we asked them to pull the master oil chip detector and it had metal shavings on it. With the oil temp over limit that requires an engine change.I'm not sure we can prevent this kind of failure this was a really oddball problem we have not seen before. I think we were a victim of a failing lube and scavenge pump or gearbox the oil may have been hiding in the gearbox. If we were to do this again I may have asked MX to do a high power run instead of just an idle run; But it may not have shown the problem.

column121: I performed my pre-flight check before flying the Mavic 2 Pro drone. My mission was to capture photos from each corner of the property and over the swimming pool area. My usual pre-flight check list before every flight is:1. Check for any airspace restrictions; TFR; NFLZ; any max altitude requirements; etc.2. Request approval with FAA if my location would be in any controlled airspace (my location was not in controlled airspace).3. Be sure all 4 propellers are secure and not damaged.4. Battery is fully charged.5. Check for any magnetic interference.6. Set my RTH.7. Make sure drone is connected to controller.8. Be sure my remote pilot license and current certificates are on or next to me before flying.9. Take off and hover drone to about 5 feet and check that all controls are functioning.10. Fly mission.I recalibrate the drone after about every 6 to 8 flights. This was my 6th flight before I would recalibrate again before the next flight or two.Before taking off; the property manager and I had people that were swimming in the pool move to a covered area temporarily for their safety.The property manager was not part of the mission and not a VO (visual Observer). I performed my pre-flight check; and I began my mission and captured a couple of photos of the swimming pool area first at 380 feet or 116 meters directly above the pool. I was controlling the drone from the ground inside the pool area.Next; I flew the drone South to the back of the property to take pictures of the playground area. As I was flying the drone to where I wanted to go; the property manager watched over my shoulder at my controller screen to see the view of the property. Once I flew over the playground; I yawed the drone 180 degrees to frame up the playground in my camera with the rest of the property. At this point; the drone was hovering at 357 feet (109 meters) above a wide open area of land with trees with the camera pointing North West. I took my photos; then I yawed to face the camera West and began flying to the next corner of the property to where I would yaw to point the camera North East for the photos. (The pool area would be the far North East corner where I was controlling the drone from this angle when I would take the photos.)About 5 seconds into this direction (West); my controller beeped; and I looked down. The property manager was still watching the controller.  We saw the camera on the drone flip up at the propellers and the app froze. The Kittyhawk app (now called Aloft) displayed 'Drone Disconnected' at the top of the screen. I quickly hit the RTH button on the controller; but the app was still displaying 'Drone Disconnected' and the RTH button would not activate. At this time; I looked up to find the drone; but I could not see it anymore. Since the controller disconnected from the drone; I presumed the drone fell to the ground; and the property manager and I (and two of her maintenance workers) performed a search where we thought the drone may have crash landed in the fields.We notified the owner of the land where we were searching as well as a restaurant closest to the fields and asked them to be aware of a possible drone on the ground or in the trees and to notify us if they find it. I also tried connecting the controller to the drone while we searched; but it would never reconnect.The weather was partly cloudy; 92 degrees; and Wind 7 mph during the flight. Further south where I took pictures from the playground area were two towers; but the drone was nowhere near them.The drone did not log the duration of flight; but it was about three or four minutes into the flight when the malfunction occurred.

column121: [The] flight departed ZZZ; [runway] XXL and at 400 ft. we were given a heading of 360. As soon as the turn was initiated a loud bang was heard from below and behind the cockpit. The noise then went away. A few moments later FA (Flight Attendant) 1 called up and reported a loud banging noise from 2R. There were no ECAM or any other indications in the cockpit - all displays were normal - nor was the noise audible from the cockpit. After getting the airplane stabilized and the after-takeoff checks completed; I sent the FO (First Officer) back to investigate. It was confirmed that a loud banging was obvious in the cabin. A return to the field was planned; ATC notified; [priority handling was requested]; FA's briefed for a precautionary landing; Dispatch notified and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) requested. Runway XY was requested as this was an overweight landing; and the QRH procedure was followed. A smooth landing followed; the aircraft was brought to a stop after clearing Runway XY and the airplane inspected by CFR crew. The comment was that; 'A door was missing.' No other damage noted; and the flight taxied to a gate uneventfully. A walk-around revealed the 2R slide door departed the aircraft; followed by the slide. The noise was from the inflation supply line which was banging against the fuselage and wing root. A write-up for the missing door and raft was entered into the log along with the overweight landing notes. [The cause can be found through] perhaps confirmation of all maintenance items accomplished during the inspection at ZZZ immediately previous to this event. [I suggest to find the] determination of why the slide/raft door failed and [to find] appropriate remedies [to be] taken to preclude future issues.
column123: I was assigned FO (First Officer) on [the] flight. I arrived at aircraft and the Captain was already at the aircraft. I performed the preflight walk-around and noted no issues. All checks for preflight were normal. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XXL; initial climb to 5000 and heading 290. Takeoff was normal. The Captain called for AP (Autopilot) on and pulled heading at turn altitude. Climb power reduction and clean-up was normal. We were handed off to Departure and checked in. Departure gave us a climb to 7;000 and 360 heading. I confirmed 7;000 with ATC and the Captain set 7;000 and I confirmed it. As he turned the heading knob to 360; a loud bang was heard from behind the flight deck. The #1 FA (Flight Attendant) called and reported the bang and a clunking noise near 2R door. No ECAM or warnings were displayed.The Captain retained the aircraft; leveled at 16;000 as cleared; and set speed to 245. We completed all checks and asked ATC to remain at 16000 as we needed to check out something. They approved that and asked if we were [requesting priority handling]. We replied not at this time; but we will need to check some things. The Captain then asked if I was OK with going back and checking things out as the sound could not be heard on the flight deck. The FA came forward and I went to the cabin and inspected the area and heard the banging she described. I returned to the flight deck; described what I heard and what I felt was happening and suggested that we return. The Captain agreed and formulated a return plan. He completed all notifications [and] reviewed all procedures with me. We [requested priority handling] and returned to base for an overweight landing.The Captain performed the landing as per QRH procedures. He brought the aircraft to a stop on the taxiway as CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) could inspect the aircraft; and they informed us that there was a door open and everything else looked OK. We taxied to the gate; followed shutdown procedures; and then went down to inspect the aircraft. At that time; we found that the 2R slide door and slide were missing and the inflation hose was hanging down and had struck the fuselage. The Captain the entered entries in the AML for the damage and overweight landing.My concern is that when we checked the system pages to see if we had any systems issues; there were none indicated. The doors page showed all the slides green and the white 'slide' indications. I.e.; normal armed condition. Had the green box that indicated the 2R slide shown amber; we would have been alerted that the door was in fact open - in this case gone - and would have had a better idea of what we were dealing with.

column121: I was coming back to my home airport after a fuel stop; there was weather coming in and I was trying to land before the storm got to the airport. I entered pattern at a 45 degree entrance to the downwind of Runway XX and flew the rest of the pattern. On short final; I was at landing speed of 90MPH. I landed long on the runway and tapped the brakes on landing which entered my aircraft into a porpoise. Being too far down the runway; I knew I could not pull out of it and needed to keep the airplane on the ground. I pulled the power to keep it down and the prop struck the ground which then collapsed the nose gear and brought me to a stop. Analyzing the situation; the first mistake I made was trying to beat the storm. This was the root to everything that happened. Next; I was coming down too fast and landed too long. I also tapped the brakes; which commenced the porpoise. If I was put into this situation again; I would have diverted to another close airport and waited for the storm to pass. What I have learned from this is to never try to beat a storm; along with don't rush to get down and go around when you need to go around. I am very lucky to have walked away from this situation and it will forever be an experience to learn from and never repeat.

column121: We arrived at ZZZ Gate at approximately XA:30. Upon arriving at the gate there were no ramp personnel in the area. We parked as directed by the DGS system; shut down the engines; and performed the Shutdown Checklist (including 'Brakes Set'). After a few minutes; (indicated by the cargo doors opening on the ECAM) ground personnel approached the aircraft to perform their duties. I left my seat to use the lavatory and to assure the #1 Flight Attendant (FA) and our First Class passengers that we were diligently trying to find someone to open the door. Approximately 10-15 minutes later; the agent opened the door. I returned to the flight deck to gather my belongings before saying goodbye to the passengers at the door. We never received the 'chocks in' hand signal and had no ground power connected despite our efforts to get it done. In the mean time; shortly after main cabin door opening; a maintenance tech came up to the flight deck and gathered some pins from the gear pin stowage compartment; for what he indicated was some sort of inspection. I was called the next morning and informed by the ZZZ1 Director of Flight that while we were on the flight deck we had an aircraft rollback causing damage to the jet bridge. Not one person on or near the aircraft indicated that we had any aircraft movement and First Officer (FO) and I were totally unaware of the rollback. Often we arrive at the gate and there are no ramp personnel to chock the airplane. In addition; very shortly after door opening; there is a maintenance technician present to perform required operational inspections. As the flight deck crew; we performed our required post flight duties. We cannot account for the other several departments involved in the safe securing of the aircraft. As the Pilot-in-Command (PIC) of the aircraft; I sincerely believe that the parking brake was set. Given the intense scheduling practices and understaffing of the airline on the Aircraft Maintenance Department and Customer Service; along with the obvious poor training of Ground Support; I have no idea what happened.

Marshalers parked us; said chocks were set and captain pointed at the screen; and I turned the APU on (both engines still running at this point). Both engines were at idle. Around 30% spin up; felt a shunt and heard a noise from the right side of the cabin. Captain asked what that was; I thought it was the APU conking out (plane had been written up for a recirculation fan issue when we got it; and the only change we'd made was the APU turning). Captain asked if it was a baggage cart that had hit us or something; so I started looking around. Looked out and saw ground crew looking around and looking at engine 2. After the APU reached 100% and the engines were shut down; I (First Officer) opened the window and asked what happened; to which the ground crew said a cone went into the engine. Captain immediately sent message to Dispatch and was on the phone with company as I waited for the jet bridge to connect so I could do my walk around.When doing my walk around; asked the ground crew person who was handling the cone what happened; he said he 'got close to the engine; then something didn't feel right - like the cone was pulling'. He said he then 'pulled back; and that's when the cone got sucked into the engine'. It was an orange cone connected by a pipe. The cone closest to the engine had been sucked in. I did notice the ramper in question had Bose headphones around his head but not over his ears when I was talking to him. Don't know if that was a factor.On walk around; found most of the cone behind the intake; pieces in the stator vanes; and debris strewn across the ramp. Pieces found behind Left Main Landing Gear; and about as far back as about 30 feet behind the tail of the plane. No damage noted to landing gears or tires. Captain came out and also assessed the damage; and we informed the next crew of the situation as well.APU could have been turned on sooner to allow engine to be shut down quicker. Ramp crew should wait to approach engines until they're shut down.
column123: We landed in ZZZ on Runway XX. The taxi to our planned gate; Gate XX; was short. The engines had not passed the 2-minute cool-down prior to entering the ramp. First Officer then tried to reach Operations via radio at least twice but didn't get a response. Simultaneously; I was being marshalled to Gate XY so we proceeded to park at Gate XY. I parked at the gate without incident and set the parking brake. I looked down and noticed the APU had not yet started and pointed it out to the First Officer. Between the cool-down period; trying to verify the gate; and watching for obstacles on the ramp; the APU had not yet been started. The engines were idle while the APU was starting. At approximately 20-30% APU; we felt an impact on the right side of the aircraft; followed by a loud noise. I asked what happened. There were no EICAS or gauge indications of a problem. The First Officer thought maybe the APU malfunctioned during the start and I asked if a baggage cart impacted the aircraft. Around this time the marshaller started looking toward Engine 2. When the APU reached 100% I shut both engines down. The First Officer opened his window and asked what happened. The ground crew indicated that ENG 2 had ingested an orange traffic cone. I immediately sent an ACARS to dispatch and called Maintenance to report the incident. The First Officer conducted his walk-around and assessed the ENG 2 damage; taking pictures which he sent to Maintenance via e-mail. Upon his return; the First Officer provided the following explanation from the employee who placed the cone:The ramper allegedly explained that as he went to place the cones in front of ENG 2; two orange pyramid-shaped traffic cones connected by a white plastic pipe; he felt the engine start to ingest the cone furthest from him. He stepped back but the cone didn't stay connected to the pipe. The First Officer noted that the ramper responsible for cone placement was wearing a Bose headset. This is extremely uncommon. So uncommon that I've never seen a ramp worker with a Bose headset or similar headset capable of playing music. I do not know if anything was interfering with the ramp worker's ability to properly hear the aircraft engines. After the APU was off and the airplane was connected to the GPU; I conducted a visual inspection of ENG 2 and called maintenance with an update of the ground crew's explanation of how the cone was ingested. I made a video recording of the fan blades. During this time; the ramp worker was telling the First Officer that he wasn't sure whether or not he should have told us to shut-down the engine when the cone was ingested. Ground crew should be trained to recognize when an engine is on and when to notify the crew to immediately shut the engine down. The ramp worker could have been killed due to his lack of training in recognizing an operating engine.  Engines can be running at the gate for any number of valid reasons and ground crew should be trained when to recognize an operating engine. Ground crew should be properly trained in hand signals for an abnormality. Pilots could wait to taxi into the gate until the 2-minute cool down passes and the APU is operational to further prevent these kind of incidents.

column121: During push with brake set; started the Right Engine. Immediately after the engine started; we received an APU Limit checklist indication. We ran the checklist which stated an exceedance had occurred and directed us to shutdown the APU; which we did. Shortly after shutting down the APU with the overhead switch; the ground mechanic stated on the intercom 'APU fire; shutdown the APU.' I then stated 'no we do NOT have an APU fire indication in the cockpit; but did get an APU limit checklist; which we ran and shut down the APU already.' He acknowledged the radio and I believe at this point went to the back of the airplane for a closer look. I assumed any smoke he had seen was from the limit exceedance and decided not to fire the APU bottle since we did not have an indication of an APU fire. After taking care of the switches in the cockpit; I went outside to investigate what had occurred and found two mechanics at the rear of the airplane with the APU compartment open; as they investigated the APU from a cherry-picker stand. From the ground; I could see no evidence of any fire either inside the APU compartment nor on the exterior of the tail section. When finished with their examination; the mechanics came into the cockpit to explain what they found. I had great difficulty understanding their English and exactly what they were saying; except that they would now MEL the APU. I understood them to say they thought it was from fluid leaking in the APU. I only found out after talking to the operations director on a phone patch on the ramp in ZZZZ; that the mechanics had used a fire extinguisher during their inspection. They did not tell me this or perhaps both my First Officer and I misunderstood them. I did not witness them using a fire extinguisher and it must have occurred prior to me leaving the cockpit to investigate. I made a write-up in the logbook. No emergency was declared because it seemed well under control. Better communication between crew and mechanics over what they did; as they should have told the Captain that a fire extinguisher was used! Now perhaps they did attempt to tell the crew and we did not comprehend what they were stating.
