column121: Preflight and runup was normal. Engine operation was good. Began taxiing on the runway. Full power was applied and engine instruments were all in the green (RPM; pressure; and temperature). Airspeed was increasing slowly initially at first; but RPM increased as airspeed increased and I reached rotation speed of 60 to 65. I reached my normal Vx speed of 65 to 70 MPH. I had seen the climb-out of another aircraft and it appeared to be windy so I decided to add a little more speed to that as a buffer for safety. I had briefed this prior to takeoff and was aiming for 70 to 75 for the climb out; for obstacle avoidance and wind buffer. I also had briefed and prepared for a wind shift as I got above the trees; as this is a standard precaution that I have regularly made at this airport (because of the location of the trees) and was prepared to expect it (as is regularly briefed for an eventuality such as this). This is a part of my normal before takeoff emergency brief. As soon as I got nearing the tops of the trees I felt the lift reduce and the stall horn began. The controls were sluggish and I knew instantly that I needed to lower the nose to prevent a stall. I lowered the nose and tried to nurse it back up but very quickly realized something needed to be done as the runway was reducing and I didn't feel comfortable in the lift being generated being able to take me over the trees. I made a quick decision to reduce the power and attempt for an aborted landing. I pitched over; touched down; and hit the brakes. I realized that the runway was coming to an end and the hill was going to slope down. So I attempted to turn the aircraft using the rudders and was successful in slowing the aircraft and not going down into the sloped hill. Then; managed to stop the aircraft at the end of the runway. Once the aircraft was stopped; the engine was running; I pulled the mixture; switched the mags to off; and turned off the master. Post-incident inspection showed apparently minor prop damage (a ding in the prop) and nothing else appeared to be damaged. Postflight discussion with the pilot of the initial observed aircraft and he stated that he also felt the wind shift and was struggling to climb. The climbout seemed a little low to me; but it was not readily apparent to me that it was solely because of the winds. I surmise that a windshear event occurred from the changing wind direction because of the trees. Luckily; I had briefed for this eventuality and knew what to do. Things that went right:- Proper brief prior to takeoff which covered a change in wind due to the trees- Proper speed-wind buffer: this resulted in the lift that WAS available at that time and contributed to a safe landing without exceeding the critical Angle of Attack.  - Managed to stop the aircraft with minimal damage; and no occupant damageThings that went wrong:- Initial observation of the struggling climb of the aircraft on departure should have resulted in more hesitancy to depart to begin with

column121: I am the owner of a Mooney M20E and have >300 hours in this plane. The flight in the late afternoon was a demonstration flight for a friend of mine who is considering beginning pilot training. He has done informal training many times over several years including with me; and has excellent instincts and innate skills that indicate he will be an excellent pilot. In addition; he has significant knowledge about airplanes; airplane systems and general aeronautical/ aviation information. Weather conditions were VFR and not challenging in any way. There were some mild clouds and precipitation in the area but we had no difficulty avoiding them throughout the flight.I flew left seat and handled all engine controls and critical phases of flight; takeoffs; landings; radio calls; etc. He had controls for much of the enroute time and legs of traffic patterns. We did standard maneuvers; mostly practice traffic patterns and landings at ZZZ1; which is close to ZZZ and is the most commonly used training field for many pilots out of ZZZ; including myself. We did three touch and goes and one full stop/ taxi back at ZZZ1. There was no indication of a gear problem for any of these several extensions or retractions. I have very recently done solo training flights with similar or greater numbers of gear extensions and retractions in a similar span of time with no indication of problem. After close to an hour of flying; we returned toward ZZZ for our final stop. We entered a long right base for Runway XXR; and at the appropriate time put the gear switch down. For the first time ever in this plane that I know of; there was a gear extension problem. The gear motor activated and could be felt extending the gear. It seemed mostly normal; but perhaps a little louder/ more forceful than usual. It stopped abruptly; it seemed to have taken a usual amount of time; but the gear on this plane do normally extend quickly and I could not be certain the motor had run as long as usual. The two gear down lights (one on the panel and one on the floor) did not illuminate. The gear actuator circuit breaker had popped out. I tried resetting the circuit breaker twice; but it did not stay in. The gear switch had no effect at this point; as expected with the circuit breaker tripped. The feel of the plane in flight felt as though the gear were down with the expected amount of drag.I advised ZZZ tower that we were breaking off the approach for troubleshooting of a gear problem; and headed generally north of the field in coordination with the controller. I pulled out the Owner's Manual; and my passenger assisted in reviewing the manual gear extension procedure; with which I am very familiar. I have practiced this on the ground a few times over the years at the time of annual inspection with the plane on jacks. I have also practiced it in the air at least once in this plane.With my passenger reviewing the steps out loud for me; I extended the gear manually. The hand crank did not reach a stopping point and the gear down lights did not illuminate. I checked the visual floor indicator; which is there as a backup in case of electrical failure; and the 'GEAR DOWN' sign was visible as normal when the gear extend; with the alignment bars lined up normally as per my memory of how they typically line up. Many additional cranks on the manual extension handle on several more tries had no further effect on anything that I could tell. We were concerned we might have a broader electrical problem of some type leading to failure of the indicator lights; even though the gear appeared to be fully extended. I checked another indicator light on the panel in the same cluster as the 'Gear Down' light (the 'Ram Air' light); which was working properly. I could find no other signs of electrical failure on board. There was no smell or sign of smoke.At this point; I contacted ZZZ tower and coordinated a low pass down Runway XXR to get a visual check of the gear. The tower controller was ableto see the gear well and reported all three appeared to be fully extended. The plane was performing well and maintaining control was not an issue. I was able to aviate; navigate and communicate easily and without difficulty; and to go through the appropriate manual gear extension procedure with plenty of time and focus. My passenger remained very calm; focused and helpful throughout. Neither of us became anxious or nervous; and we were able to communicate well and work together well. He was an asset to me functioning as part of the crew; even without formal pilot training. The ZZZ controller(s) likewise were extremely responsive; helpful and professional.I did not seem to have any additional options to try to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate. I was fairly confident that the gear were fully extended. We were in no immediate danger; and there seemed to be no other emergency reason to land prematurely; although the possibility of some larger electrical system problem remained in my mind. As such; I decided that spending extra time in the air for additional attempts at troubleshooting was no longer wise and that we should land safely while conditions were good.The landing on Runway XXR was smooth; well controlled and uneventful. The wind was nearly straight down the runway and was light. I most often land with no flaps; and chose to do so in this case as well. I made sure to land with excellent technique; touching down gently just above stall speed; well aligned with the center line and with minimal control inputs. I made sure not to use the brakes; and I elected not to use the elevator for aerodynamic braking; as I wanted to avoid any unnecessary forces on the gear. I allowed the plane to roll out long on the runway; and all appeared to be going well. I let the tower know that I intended to roll out long due to the unknown status of the gear. Runway XXR is 7;500 feet long; I touched down not far past the numbers; and rolled out nearly to taxiway 1 for a total rollout distance of about 3;500-4;000 feet.After we had dissipated most of our forward speed without incident or sign of additional problem; I began a very gentle right turn toward the 'high speed' exit for taxiway 1. At that point; the plane began to settle toward the ground toward the left; with the front and right settling down very quickly after. The prop struck the runway and the engine quit; the plane skidded about 30 feet and came to a stop at a mild angle off center line. The impact with the runway was surprisingly soft from our standpoint. I quickly shut off the master switch; magneto switches; and fuel selector; and we exited the plane quickly and easily. There was no fuel spillage; smoke or fire. Neither of us sustained any injury of any kind.Using a heavy boom truck; we were able to gently lift the plane off the runway via the engine mount. I was able to easily manually extend the gear fully; and again was unable to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate despite the gear being verified fully down; and the manual floor indicator properly aligned. While being towed away; the plane again settled to the ground toward the left when initiating a fairly gentle slow turn to the right. This time; only the left gear folded.At the time; shortly after; and for the next day or two I believed that I had properly pushed the crank forward to engage the manual gear extension mechanism and allow the handle to work properly. This is one of the basic few steps needed in the manual gear extension procedure; and I had done it many times. It is a small handle and lever located at approximately the left side of the left pilot's knee; and is easily reachable with your left hand. After reflecting on the events and going back to visit the plane; in fact I had not properly pushed that lever all the way forward. It appears that the manual gear extension mechanism will apply enough lowering force even when not properly engaged to allow the gear to fully or nearly fullyextend; but without the crank properly engaged it appears that you cannot get enough force to fully lock the gear in place.At the time of the [event]; although I and my passenger were under good control and responding well to the situation; I was approaching or beyond 14 hours since I had woken up and gone to work early that morning. I believe that pushing the end of my duty day; as well as familiarity with the procedure and not double checking myself that I had followed every step properly were contributing factors in my failure to fully lock the gear. I believe I could have prevented the gear collapse had I followed the checklist and double checked every step.We have not yet jacked the plane and examined all of the relevant components. Whether or not there is some other structural damage to the gear extension mechanism or any of the components involved; and whether or not we are able to ultimately demonstrate that the gear down lights were or were not in fact working; it does not change the fact that I did not properly complete one of the necessary steps on the checklist for manual gear extension. I also failed to catch this omission with a thorough review of the procedure and circumstances after the gear lights failed to come on. I allowed myself to give too much weight to the possibility of an indicator failure and did not continue to troubleshoot more when I have the ability to do so. I also believed that my familiarity with the procedure was sufficient that I did not consider that I might have omitted or failed to properly complete a step.As I reflect on this; it gives me a sense of humility and a reminder of my own fallibility; and reinforces that I need to double check checklists and critical steps at all times. My belief that my left hand had done what it was supposed to with respect to the one missing step was simply inaccurate. I could have and should have caught the error with a careful review of the circumstances; and there was not an emergency pressing need to get the plane on the ground immediately. I will carry this lesson for the rest of my life. Fortunately; no one was injured; and the mechanical and financial damage to the plane are the only costs. But it is still a humbling fact that I did a basic part of managing my aircraft incorrectly and caused damage as a result. In another circumstance; I or someone else could have been hurt with such an error. I will redouble my efforts to be meticulous for procedures; checklists; and review of critical items at all times. In addition; I will be more careful with respect to aircraft operations beyond 12 or 13 hours since waking up in the morning on any particular occasion.

column121: During the preflight of the aircraft; my student performed the inspection. He called me in when he was having trouble removing the oil dipstick of the right engine to inspect oil level since it was secured very tight and was hot to the touch. I came out there with a napkin to use as an insulator for our fingers and managed to loosen the dipstick by using both my hands. I checked the oil level and handed the dipstick to the student for him to do the same. He placed the dipstick back in and secured it; and I doubled checked that the stick was secure by loosening and retightening it. I then proceeded to run my own quick check of the aircraft by verifying the oil in the left engine and checking the fuel quantity onboard. We found no issues with the aircraft and proceeded with the flight.About an hour into the flight; we were in the south practice area performing Vmc demo with the student at the controls. During the maneuver; I had noticed an oil slick starting to form off the right engine. For the maneuver; we were operating the right engine at full power while the left was idle. To make sure we are all on the same page; I pointed out the slick and had him start turning back to ZZZ. I instructed him to scissor the throttles; go full power on the left engine and idle the right engine. I immediately called up our dispatch and informed them of our engine trouble while they coordinated preparations at the school; airport; and rescue services as part of the company procedures. About three minutes after we idled the right engine; the oil temperature was rising to the limit. Since we were holding 3;000 feet at the time with an idling engine with good performance; and I did not want to risk having a seized engine I elected to shut the engine down and feather it. We informed dispatch; and then followed the appropriate checklist. And elected to continue to ZZZ since they still needed time to prepare the field for our arrival with emergency services; familiarity; and long runways available. On the way back; I shifted my attention to the student and briefed what happened; and what we are going to do from now. During this time; I had him at the controls flying while I ran the checklists with him. I briefed that I would have him fly to ZZZ but once we start maneuvering; I will take the controls for descent and landing. As we were nearing the field; dispatch called us requesting we circle the field if performance allows for a few minutes while they still waited for rescue to arrive. Once we were about 3 miles south at 3;000 [feet]; dispatch called again telling we do not need to circle anymore; and that the airport will not call rescue. I really did not want to stay in the air longer than we needed to; and changing the plan now would have increased risks; I opted to continue to land. I took the controls at this point; and since we needed to lose altitude; I decided to fly a normal pattern and flew down to make a normal 45 entry for runway 20. Runway 20 was the longest runway with most favorable wind conditions. The landing was successful. The airport was closed for our recovery; and we planned to shut down on the runway and get a tow; but I was nervous about another aircraft behind me on short final; so I used the remaining speed of the aircraft to turn off onto the taxiway at about 10 knots.During the post flight inspection; we could not see anything out of place other than the oil streaks. We checked the dipstick and saw that it had slightly loosen but appear to be seated. But when maintenance performed their inspection; they determined the oil dipstick was cross threaded. They determined this was the most likely source of the oil leak. Only about a quart of oil was lost in flight.I think obviously the biggest factor here was the dipstick not secured properly. I was not aware how easily the dipstick could be cross threaded. The biggest learning moment for me was paying closer attention to how the dipstick is seated. In the specific aircraft; the dipstick sits directly on the engine block; and you can only easily see the dipstick from a top view unlike other aircraft I operate such as the other [aircraft type] where the dipstick is sits on a pipe that protrudes from the engine where the dipsticks cap is visible from the side. I think what also did not help was the fact we used a napkin to hold the dipstick during the preflight; which also visibly covered it. I think from here on out I am going to make sure some gloves are accessible and emphasize to my students the potential risk of cross threading.However; I am concerned about the airports handling of this situation. It was revealed when we landed; the airport management seemed to have not deemed our situation important enough to call in fire rescue as a precaution. They also have seemed to do a poor job of closing the airport as aircraft were still taking off and landing even when they announced multiple times over the radio the airport is closed. When I landed; a aircraft was flying not too far behind us in the pattern; and I had to move the aircraft on a single engine off the runway out of concern they would land on top of us which added the risk to us. But in the end of the day; the aircraft made it back in one piece; and most importantly my student and I made back safe.

column121: There had been a ground stop for passing storms to the east; which were now 1/3 of the way between ZZZ and ZZZ1. The Captain gave a briefing and asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated the entire flight due to the cells we'd be flying around and the potential for turbulence. He also made this part of his welcome aboard announcement.We took off and were given a 090 heading; transitioning north of the group of cells. This group of cells gave us a small option north toward ZZZ2 VOR and a small option south between cells. Neither path had a significant advantage over the other.Once we were abeam the northern track; ATC gave us a hole they depicted on their radar to our 1 o'clock position. We opted to continue straight; but ATC said straight looked worse to them. We conversed back and forth with them and the hole appeared to our right and clear skies on the back side. We maneuvered right; then left to make a perpendicular path through the hole. The bottom of the hole was higher than our altitude and we were given a climb from 17;000 to FL210. We tried to establish this climb at 250 kts. to stay slow for possible turbulence. This was made difficult by the fact we had an MEL for the speed bug. The speed bug jumped from the upper 200s into the lower 300s; back and forth throughout the flight. It was distracting and was the first time either of us had experienced this particular anomaly in nearly four years. Just prior to penetration; we could see heavy lightning coming from the cells immediately left of our path; extending toward the area we were originally going toward.As we climbed to FL210; we penetrated the lower portion of the hole and into IMC. Throughout the encounter; we had moderate turbulence and heavy to extreme rain. Our ice detection caution message activated; as well.We estimate the pass took 30 to 45 seconds to transition. I tried to transmit to ATC not to send anyone behind us; but never received a response.Once in clear air; I tried ATC again and they said they'd been trying to reach us to say the hole had closed up on their scope. We never their transmission either.In discussion after passing into clear air; neither of us felt we'd encountered hail. The sound of the rain striking the window and body of the aircraft were consistent with heavy to extreme rain.I checked on the Flight Attendants to make sure they were ok and to make sure the passengers were ok; and everyone was. We landed without incident and discovered damage during the walk around.The first area I noticed was the radome. There were extensive areas where the paint had been removed and the composite material underneath was exposed. There were three areas where horizontal slices in the composite material were visible. There was at least one area where a circular area was compromised. Most of the damaged paint and material were on the upper half of the radome. There was one hole that was previously covered during the preflight inspection that was now exposed due to speed tape coming off the aircraft. We conducted numerous; slow and methodical visual inspections of the exterior of the aircraft over the course of the next two hours. The only other damage was an unidentified antenna on the top of the aircraft. It was located aft of the VHF 1 antenna and forward of the upper beacon. POH and PRM (Pilot's Reference Manual) searches failed to produce an identity to this antenna; and might possibly be a wifi antenna installed after manufacturer documents were printed.The Captain notified [Maintenance Control]; the Chief Pilots; and Dispatch and briefed them on the incident and the status of the aircraft. Our Contract Maintenance arrived about an hour later and began making an evaluation of the damage. Our return flight was eventually cancelled and we rode the brakes for Ground Personnel while they repositioned the aircraft. We left the aircraft with Maintenance and proceeded to the hotel. After the flight; the Captain and I debriefed our flight and the incident. The flight attendants and the passengers were secured at the time due to crew briefings and the announcement that the seat belt sign would stay on and the flight attendants would remain seated throughout the flight. As previously noted; we had north and south options that were basically equal. Since our radar conflicted somewhat with ATC; we applied their observations into our decision making process in accordance with good CRM procedures. We had convection on our left and right sides and clear blue skies ahead. Our ability to climb over the IMC we entered could have been better facilitated if we began our climb sooner; however there was a small layer that obstructed our view and we were too close to the hole when the height of that IMC was determined. column121: Since we have taken delivery of more 737 Max aircraft; I have noticed that aircraft are coming with the aircraft headset attached to the sidewall of the aircraft.  The method this is accomplished; wires the headset wires into position near the headset jacks in such a manner that they cannot be removed.  The problem starts when pilots open the window; to talk with ground crew; ventilation; wing inspection; etc.  At this point; the wire becomes tangled; and stuck in the window mechanism.  The result is that the window is not completely closed; or that the headset cord is damaged; requiring replacement.  In addition to the costly factors above; if a crew were required to egress through the window; its possible the additional tanglements from the wire might prevent the window from opening completely.In the past month; I have personally observed two maintenance write-ups where damage occurred to the headset wire. One was on the FO (First Officer) side; one on the Captains side.  An additional write up involved a return to field; because the window wasn't properly closed despite the window handle being over center.There is no requirement to wire into position the headset (most of which are unused by pilots anyway).  Many other airlines fleet do not have the headset wired into position in this manner.

column121: This report concerns the unscheduled separation of the #4 - outboard right main wheel - from the aircraft on takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ. We began the trip receiving the aircraft from the previous crew at the gate in ZZZ1 one leg prior. There were no abnormalities on the pre-flight; no abnormalities that had not been cleared; and no major abnormalities of any kind recorded in the logbook or in the previous logbook that was in the can for the aircraft. The previous crew verbally told us that it was performing well when we received it from them. The first leg; ZZZ1 to ZZZ; operated smoothly with nothing out of the ordinary occurring. The post flight after that leg revealed no discrepancies of any kind. We pushed back from ZZZ; and our taxi route towards Runway XX included left- and right-hand turns as well as brake applications; and the aircraft continued to operate normally with no signs of any abnormality on the wheels.When we performed the takeoff; shortly after we selected the landing gear up; Tower called us and told us it looked like we lost a tire on the runway. The takeoff was so smooth that we weren't sure if we had in fact lost a tire as we had no indication in the cockpit of any system abnormalities; and the aircraft felt like it was operating normally. We knew there was construction around the runway in about the position we would have lifted off the ground at; so I thought that perhaps it was misidentified construction debris - although we hadn't seen any debris on the runway prior to takeoff. We asked them to perform a runway inspection to determine if it was our tire while we contacted Dispatch to obtain some identifying information about it; as well as to make a plan of action in case it was our tire. We contacted ZZZ Operations after some attempts; and asked them to remain at the airport to assist in identifying the tire and in case we needed to return to ZZZ.We decided not to relay to Dispatch through Operations because we initially had trouble reaching them and we believed that their Operations radio was a handheld and would not have good signal at altitude and location we would need to hold at. We decided to continue climb so that we could contact Dispatch through AIRINC. We discussed the possibility of flying by ZZZ Tower to have them identify if we were missing the tire and which one it was; but at that time we were still not sure that it was our tire and we were unsure if we would have enough fuel to do that and still proceed to ZZZ1 if that was what Dispatch wanted us to do. We made the judgement call that Dispatch would most likely have us continue to ZZZ1 due to the long runways; good emergency services; and having the finest Operations and Maintenance staff there to assist. We continued to climb along our filed route while ATC attempted to identify the tire. Shortly after that; we advised the Flight Attendant (FA) of the potential situation and that we were most likely continuing to ZZZ1; and we would wait to advise the passengers until we were sure and close to ZZZ1 to avoid panic. She said that she would take the time to review some information in her manuals. We chose to continue at a speed of long-range cruise or slower - 180 IAS being the safe speed used when structural damage is suspected - because we were unsure if there was debris on the wheel assembly that could become dislodged and damage something else; or if losing the tire had already damaged something.It took about 30 minutes to 45 minutes for us to make contact with Dispatch after that. We attempted AIRINC; Station Operations on 4 or 5 different local frequencies; relaying through company aircraft; or through another frequency. We attempted using different transmitters in case there was debris from the tire that had damaged an antenna. We were unsuccessful; so ATC attempted to call Dispatch. This took time because ATC was attempting to call using an old company number with an old area code. It was further delayed because we werebeing handed off to new controllers periodically and we had to apprise them each of the situation and have them attempt to make contact. ATC did make contact and Dispatch instructed us to continue towards ZZZ1. After that; we were advised that it was in fact our tire. We requested priority handling and continued to ZZZ1. After this determination; it took roughly 15 - 30 minutes longer for us to contact Dispatch on AIRINC.We had time with a low workload in cruise because we couldn't contact Dispatch through AIRINC yet; so we used the time to review our manuals and the QRH for the related procedures. In the QRH we decided that the Landing with Abnormal Landing Gear Procedure was the most applicable. We began to brief and discuss this procedure while trying to make contact with Dispatch through AIRINC. When we did make contact with Dispatch; [they] advised us that they thought it was the #1 wheel - the left main outboard. We told him that the procedure called to induce a fuel imbalance and to burn off as much fuel as possible before landing. We asked his opinion of going into holding on the way in to ZZZ1 to do so; and he agreed.After this determination was made; we said we would call back again and terminated the call because our radio transmitters made it very difficult to talk to ATC and Dispatch at the same time - there appeared to be interference or override between VHF 1 and 2. We began cross-feeding fuel to make the left side as light as possible and briefed the FA assuming that the #1 wheel was the one we had lost. We told the FA that there was a good chance that it would be a normal precautionary landing and that we would most likely come to a stop on the runway; or exit the runway if able; but most likely would not taxi to the gate. We decided to request for fire trucks; busses; a tug; and a GPU to be standing by. After we were done briefing the FA; we continued to discuss the procedure for approach and landing. The first step of the checklist was to notify the passengers; so we used some time to create an agreed-upon script to brief the passengers without inducing panic - which I would later administer when we were holding near ZZZ1. We noticed that this procedure appeared to be designed to cover both structural landing gear issues as well as tire and wheel problems. We were not sure if we had structural problems or not resulting from the loss of the wheel; so we briefed the procedure including several decision times - such as what we would do if the gear extended normally vs. if the gear did not extend normally vs. if we lost the hydraulic system when the gear was extended; etc. The result which did occur which we briefed was that the gear extended normally and the remaining tire; brakes; and steering operated normally for the landing.The decisions which we briefed involved in this were as follows. We left the GPWS switch in the on position because that switch's function is to silence alerts when the gear is not sensed down and locked. No fuel imbalance was established; and with our and Dispatch's agreement due to the relatively light weight of the aircraft; small practical difference the imbalance would make; and for ease of procedure application in the interest of safety. We did not pull the emergency gear extension lever due to the gear extending normally and indicating locked down by both indicating systems. Our understanding is that the emergency gear extension handle simply opens the uplock boxes; which had already been opened successfully; and that pulling the emergency gear extension handle could potentially impede us during egress if an evacuation was needed. We discussed at what time the bleeds should be selected off for approach. I had never selected the bleeds off in this aircraft in flight before; so the Captain and I had different opinions about when it should be done. We ended up selecting them off at 500 ft.; which I now agree with in hindsight. The remaining items of the checklist would be completed after we were already on the ground. We briefed that we would complete these steps if there was some kind of fire; severe damage; or loss of control evident at touchdown; but we would otherwise move slowly and discuss these steps due to the potential hazards of aircraft control involved with performing them.While we were discussing this; Dispatch called on AIRINC again and corrected that we had actually lost the #4 - outboard right main wheel - rather than the #1 as said earlier. I asked him if he was sure and made sure that Maintenance had checked the serial numbers on the wheel to be positive. After Dispatch told us this we re-briefed the Flight Attendant for the #4 wheel.After we were all thoroughly briefed; we began our delay vectors around ZZZ1 to burn down to roughly 2000 lb. as instructed by Dispatch; I gave the PA to the passengers. When we had burned enough fuel; we began the ILS to Runway XYR - the longest and most familiar runway for us in ZZZ1. The gear extended normally and we saw no abnormal flight characteristics or any system abnormalities. On touchdown; as briefed; I began using the tiller to steer the aircraft early; and we felt it pulling slightly toward the right. However; not nearly enough to warrant the emergency engine shutdown. We were able to control the aircraft throughout the rollout to maintain centerline. We chose not to try to turn off the runway as it would be a left turn-off; which would put the most weight on the right side; and we were unsure of the quality of braking that we had. We used reverse only until we were at a slow walking speed and only then used brake application to bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway centerline abeam the XX taxiway exit where the firetrucks and Operations were waiting.Tower gave us the discrete frequency to use. The firetrucks came onto the runway and asked us to shut down the #2 engine so they could inspect. We complied and they said the remaining tire seemed to be in good condition and asked us if we wanted to exit. We said no; we would like to deplane the passengers and then be tugged. While Operations was setting up to deplane the passengers; we briefed how we would manage shutting down the #1 engine in order to deplane; and requested the GPU to be connected so we could deplane with lights on without killing the batteries. When the GPU was ready; we connected; Operations pinned all 3 gears; we shut down #1; checked the after-landing and -parking checklists; called the Flight Attendant; and then began deplaning to the busses. While the passengers were deplaning; Operations connected the tug. When the passengers were clear we prepared to sit in the cockpit while Operations tugged us to Gate XX. We monitored the tug process; arrived at the gate; and began conducting the postflight inspection and filling out the logbook. I completed the logbook while the Captain called the Chief Pilot to begin debriefing.I suggest that Station Operations be provided with better radio systems; or that the ACARS system be utilized in our aircraft. It was difficult for us to establish a reliable communication with Dispatch due to a combination of poor-quality radios and not many base stations being occupied due to the time of day. A communication with Dispatch was very necessary in order for Maintenance to verify which tire was missing so that we could adjust our procedures.

column121: I took off from ZZZ in my 2008 CAW SportCruiser; an aircraft that I had recently purchased. This was my first flight from ZZZ where I had based the aircraft. I flew around the local area to familiarize myself with landmarks in a 15 NM area near ZZZ. When I returned to land; an aircraft that was returning to the airport announced their intention to land on runway XX. I set up to enter the pattern for that runway about 5 NM away and went over the approach in my mind. Then; when I was about 3 NM away; I heard a pilot announce he was entering a left downwind for runway XY. I was surprised and concerned and made changes to my power setting and flaps setting from downwind settings. I changed my approach to enter a crosswind for runway XY. I was still a little shaken by the sudden change in approach for landing. The downwind and base legs were uneventful. The final approach started well; but as I neared the runway threshold; the PAPI system indicated that I was below the glide slope. I added a little power to get back on the glide slope; but I was too far into the landing. The aircraft hit hard and then the nose gear collapsed. The aircraft slid about 250 feet on top of the nose gear fairing and cowling. The prop struck the asphalt and one blade snapped off. Fortunately; I was thoroughly strapped into the four-point restraint harness and was uninjured.In retrospect; I should have abandoned the approach when it became unstable; and initiated a go-around. This will be a very expensive lesson. I am grateful that I emerged from the experience physically unscathed.

column121: I was pilot flying; from the left seat; and the company identified PIC was pilot monitoring from the right seat. On the departure procedure from ZZZ; the right engine engine-fire light illuminated. I reduced the right throttle; as per the memory items for the indication; and the light extinguished immediately.We continued on the departure procedure and noted that the oil temperature for the right engine was at red-line. I asked the PIC/pilot monitoring to review the checklist for procedures after the memory items related to the engine fire light; while I monitored the engine gauges for other indications if a problem; radios and autopilot tracking of the departure procedure. The aircraft continued to climb within the parameters of the SID with reduced thrust on the right engine.PIC/pilot monitoring stated that we were good to continue and proceeded to look in the emergency procedures for something related to high oil temperature. PIC/pilot monitoring stated that there were no procedures or checklists for high oil temperature and that we should continue the flight at a reduced power setting on the right engine. The power setting for the right engine was about 88% N2; while the left engine was about 94% N2.PIC/pilot monitoring stated that as long as we could maintain an oil temperature below red line and climb per the SID and at a rate of at least 500 feet per minute; we should continue the departure. He did not state we should consider returning to land the aircraft.We completed the flight as he directed and called maintenance for assistance; after landing. On removing the engine cowling; significant heat damage was noted; probably from a bleed air leak; according the maintenance provider on site. Also; a metal conduit from the front to the back of the engine was found to have not been attached at the rear connecting point.Both engines were changed a week or two before this event; about 10 flight hours; ago.After the flight; I had a chance to review the procedures and found that a landing as soon as practical is called for in the procedure. This was not mentioned by the PIC.I discussed this with the PIC later in the day; and he said that he had not seen that information during the flight. Retrospectively; I am not convinced that he actually read the procedure beyond the memory items and was distracted by the high oil temperature indication and possibly by outside factors such as other work and the desire to complete the flight. PIC stated he hoped the repairs could be completed quickly so we could continue our scheduled trips in the coming days. I am also not convinced the PIC understands the gravity of his actions; or lack thereof; during this flight.There are several issues related to this event.The failure to properly install the engine was most likely the cause of the engine fire indicator light and the high oil temperature indication. I am baffled by the fact that the issue did not occur sooner after the engine change.The failure of the PIC to correctly read and follow the procedures in the emergency check list and for him to state that the flight should continue could have caused catastrophic outcome to the event.My failure; as pilot flying; to insist on an expeditious landing regardless of the checklist and the PIC's decisions; after the engine fire warning light; also decreased the chances of a successful outcome of the flight. I considered declaring an emergency and landing; but did not execute that procedure.

column121: While on a descent into ZZZ1 field I inadvertently dipped into ZZZ Class D airspace. Although I am acutely aware of the area airspace and very familiar with ZZZ; a moment of distraction due to very smokey/hazy conditions continued my descent into ZZZ Class D airspace. Upon realizing my mistake I immediately climbed up and clear of their D airspace. My best estimate is 30 seconds inside their airspace.The flight involved 2 passengers whom I invited for a flight and lunch at ZZZ2. It is clear to me that the hazy and smokey conditions contributed to my inattention. However; a much more egregious event occurred upon landing in ZZZ2 and more than anything preoccupied my thoughts. Upon arriving in the pattern at ZZZ2; there were 4 aircraft operating in a left hand pattern using Runway XX. I landed following an aircraft doing touch and goes and pulled off at the intersecting runway. I came face to face with a landing C180 who decided to use the cross runway and very narrowly avoided a collision. In the process of avoiding the landing aircraft I scraped my wingtip on a runway light. In 40 years of flying I have never dented or put a scratch in any airplane and although the damage to my wingtip is minor the event clearly preoccupied my thoughts on the way home and most likely contributed to my inattention to ZZZ's Class D airspace. In most cases when I operate around or especially under the veil our Class B airspace I set my altitude hold thus allowing me to pay more attention to traffic and other tasks. The smokey/hazy condition required hand flying to avoid pockets and areas of lesser visibility. Waiting for a better day would have been a better option.

On post flight walk around we discovered the right engine cowling was missing and a small dent in the leading edge of the tail of the aircraft. That is when we suspected that the clear air turbulence was caused by the right engine cowl departing the aircraft. ZZZ Tower; our company operations manager; and the FAA were then notified.

column121: I departed ZZZ shortly after XA00 from runway XX; heading west. Shortly after I put my gear up at approximately 100 knots airspeed and a couple hundred feet of altitude the engine started to run rough and appeared to be losing power. I made an immediate left turn to return to the runway. I was planning to land on runway XX however; the engine appeared to be losing power and airspeed. I lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and decided to attempt to make it to runway 6 with the runway lights visible. I felt that I was too low to make the runway and raised the nose to gain some attitude and give up some airspeed. At which time i heard a felt a loud bang and immediate vibration. After that point I pointed the aircraft towards the runway lights; dropped the landing gear. Although this all happened very quickly; I think a couple of minutes or so it felt as though the engine was intermittently losing and gaining power.After I landed about mid field; I was able to brake and maintain control. The vibration was mild and the engine continued to run. I stopped on the taxi way just off the runway and checked the engine gauges; verifying good oil pressure and temperature and fuel flow; was normal. I taxied to my hanger.Inspection revealed some dents in the left wing; engine cowling and damage to the 3 propeller blades. I called [an FBO] and explained the incident. He brought a replacement prop and installed it. Shortly after this I started the engine and did a run up which was all normal and smooth. I then flew the plane a couple of miles to [the FBO]. Further inspection revealed some vegetation in and around the wing gap seals. Although I did not see what I hit. I suspect it was a tree top somewhere off the airport property.

column121: I was conducting a routine cross-country flight to ZZZ1; then back to my departure location ZZZ. The flight to ZZZ1 went as planned. We landed on Runway XX and were asked to back-taxi on the runway by ATC in order for us to depart back to ZZZ. We departed from Runway XX and headed back southwest. We climbed to 4500 MSL enroute back to ZZZ. Approximately 20 miles out I began my initial descent. As I began this descent; I also tuned into the CTAF frequency as Tower was closed at this time. Approximately 10 miles out I made my first position report. I made a secondary one at 6 miles. Upon reporting at 6 miles; I was under the impression that I was the only one in the airspace as there was no other plane making reports. Upon this; I began to set up for a 6-mile final straight into Runway XX at ZZZ. I made another position report at 4 miles and then another 2 miles. Once I reached 1 mile out; I made the announcement that I was on short final. I continued my descent until I had reached the numbers and started my round out. Upon doing this; my ADS-B announced that there was traffic on short final at 6 o'clock. This traffic had not made any position reports and gave nobody in the airspace an indication for what he was doing. Upon hearing this; I made the decision to land in order to avoid a possible midair collision with this traffic.Continuing my flare; I was dealing with a 15 kt. headwind which I had flown with through my entire approach. Upon flaring; I decreased power and the wind shifted from a headwind to a crosswind that became in excess of 17 kt. As a result of this; I side-loaded my right main landing gear. As an attempt to keep the nose gear off for as long as possible; I increased power to aid in my attempt. After doing this the crosswind sheared to a tailwind; which as result forced my nose straight into the ground. With the increase in power and the direct nose impact; this resulted in the aircraft bouncing. As a result of the bounce; I initiated go-around procedures. As a I began to gain altitude; the aircraft who was not talking to anyone came to a stop on Runway XY. As a precautionary measure I flew 10 miles out and climbed up to 2500 ft. I soon turned towards the airfield and began making position reports every mile as an attempt to make contact with this aircraft. Unable to make any sort of communication with this aircraft; I overflew the field to try and see his exact position. I observed that he was off the active runway and on a taxiway. Upon noticing this; I made the decision to go in and land. This decision was based upon the fact that I was unaware of any possible damage to the aircraft and I had no exact way of telling what this other aircraft's intentions were. Upon making my base to final turn for Runway XX; this aircraft turned off the taxiway and departed Runway XY. I made a landing on XX and was able to taxi back to the hangar.As I taxied up to my hangar; this aircraft was finally able to make contact with me as he reported radio difficulties. Upon performing a normal shutdown; I got out and examined the aircraft and the only direct observation that could be made was that the tube of the front nose gear tire had gone flat. It was only once the cowling was removed that the damage to the firewall was observed. A learning experience that I will take away from this is to be more aware of potential traffic surrounding me and in my airspace. The most important one I believe is to be more aware of the possibility of windshear on final. This better preparation and awareness I believe; would help me to respond better if a situation like this were to occur again and I was called upon to take action. Having this type of experience will benefit me as before; I did not have the chance to be forced to react in a situation like this. Having gone through this will help me to learn from my mistakes and allow me to correct them and perform an appropriate response to these less-than-ideal landing conditions in the future. I also believe that I need to learn to be more hesitant about adding power in a situation like this and learn to make more accurate or precise adjustments that might be necessary.

column121: When Aircraft X from ZZZ arrived into ZZZ1; the aft cargo compartment was offloaded by my belly person Name. After the offload was complete Name informed me that there was damage to the cargo compartment. There was a metal strip that became loosened and a gap between the 2 belly panels existed along with the screw hanging. I notified control first of the aircraft damage that I needed maintenance. Manager Name1 said the rubber strip will be repaired at the end of the days flight. I told him its not the rubber strip in the floor. It was a metal strip between the belly panels. Manager Name 1 told Manager Name 2 to come to the gate to see what it was. Manager Name 2 came out a few minutes later and we showed him the video of the damage. Manager Name 2 notified the tower of the damage. Manager Name 2 told me that maintenance will come out and look at it. A short time later a collaboration between me and Manager Name 2 was that I was going to load as far as I can to the damage. The outbound load was only showing about 39 bags and it was Flight XXXX to ZZZ2. My crew and I specifically belly person Name 3 completed the load to that point and we still waited for maintenance. Name 3 was in the belly saw the damage while we waited for maintenance. At about XA:06 Manager Name 2 came to tell me that the Tower said its good to go. I told Manager Name 2 how is Tower going to tell me 'Its good to go' and to push it when no one looked at the damage. I felt that this was unsafe from what I was trained in the past. Any damage to the belly was supposed to be repaired in order to help contain a fire if one should happen to break out. I proceeded to inform the pilot in command of what the damage was. This flight was piloted by Captain A. As per the conversation he was unaware of the damage. He wanted to call maintenance to get clarification. After my conversation with the Captain; I was contacted via the radio by the Manager On Duty (MOD) Name 4. MOD Name 4 asked if I had a push crew and I said yes we are all present. Within about 5 minutes MOD Name 4 came out to Gate XX and wanted to know why we didn't push and why am I pushing 'this issue' with the flight crew. I told him that from what I was trained in the past any damage to the belly had to be repaired. Any belly damage and missing/broken/damaged nets were considered 'NO GO' items that needed to be addressed. He asked me if I was a mechanic and are you qualified to make this decision. I told him no. Then I asked him the same question in return. MOD Name 4 said no and he was told by someone (not sure who he didn't tell me) that it is good to go and will be addressed down line. He seemed to become upset with me and my decision to contact the Pilot In Command on my concerns of safety. He also wanted to see me in 'The office' later. Short time later my push driver told me the Captain wanted to talk to me again. The Captain wanted to know what's going on. I told him that MOD Name 4 is upset that we didn't follow his instruction to push. The Captain said that I did the right thing on reporting the damage and that it is his license on the line as well if something should happen. The Captain wanted to talk to MOD Name 4 on the headset. MOD Name 4 declined. I was directed by MOD Name 4 to take my lunch and talk to him later. I went inside and contacted [a] union representative. The union representative came to the ready room and I had told him what happened from my point of view. The union representative spoke to the Captain for a long period of time. After the conversation Captain and union representative both came back into the ready room and in front of my entire crew and myself; he told me I did the right thing by bringing it to his attention and he will take care of this incident on his end. I was given the Captain's information if I needed follow up. The flight eventually pushed out about 54 minutes past departure time.

column121: I rented the aircraft from the owner for an approximately 1-hour local VFR flight. A non-pilot passenger was invited to ride in the front seat for the flight. The airplane was placed on the taxiway in front of the hangar where it normally stays; and was facing northwest for the engine start. The plan was to start the engine; taxi to the fuel pumps; shut down; and top off the fuel tank. After fueling; I planned to start the aircraft and taxi to Runway XX to depart on the local VFR flight. The aircraft has no starter and a hand-prop was utilized. I was the person that hand-propped the aircraft. After hand-propping; the aircraft accelerated away and to the right; impacting the hangar door. Neither the passenger nor I were injured. Best solution is to always have the PIC in the aircraft and have a second person hand prop. In lieu of this; having substantial chocks in place would be the next best option.

column121: This occurrence happened after maneuvers. We were practicing normal takeoffs and landings at ZZZ which had a crosswind component of 10 kt. After a first attempt and go-around; we decided to try again. On the second approach in; we proceeded to come in slow; 50 kt.; and I prompted my student to add in power. However; he was frozen and too fixated to notice the low airspeed. I should have promptly issued a go-around and should have taken the controls. However; I was not forceful enough and was not able to take the controls from my student to go around; resulting in a rough landing and a tail strike. We ended up going around and did not feel there was any difference in controls and continued back to ZZZ1.Later after pushing the plane back; we noticed the damaged tail piece and the bent tail strike protection. This could have all been avoided with just a simple go-around. At the slightest feeling of something not going right - for example; not being lined up or being too slow on final - a go-around will ultimately save a bad landing from happening. The student and the instructor should always be communicating and be aware of the situation that is happening. A positive exchange of controls should be practiced frequently so that the exchange can be flawless and can prevent situations where a student may be fixated or task saturated. The reaction to go around was not quick enough and resulted in the tail strike. Task saturation is a real thing; especially if a student pilot is being introduced to a new airport and also uncontrolled airport operations as well. To wrap things up; going around is your best option and positive exchange of controls should be practiced not only when braking; but also while in the air; even in critical phases of flight.

column121: At around XA00 on Day 0; I and my colleague boarded aircraft X in the ZZZ maintenance hangar in order to take the plane to the sound wall for engine runs following maintenance. Upon starting the RH engine; a loud bang was heard and the aircraft shuddered.  We stopped the engine and talked to the lead techs who had heard the sound and immediately come over to investigate. Upon looking into the inlet; they found the remains of my coworker's hammer that had been left there; which severely damaged all the fan blades; the fan case and inlet. We shut the APU down and tugged the plane back into the hangar to assess the damage while several other mechanics were asked to walk the ramp to collect any additional FOD created by the incident.The core failure that led to the incident was lack of a proper walkaround before taking the plane outside to run. The plane had been in the hangar all night and we had been all over it inside and outside for a bi-weekly inspection; so I got complacent in assuming we knew everything we needed to know about the plane and I should focus on known sources of aircraft damage such as ground equipment and ladders; unsecured doors; safety harness ropes getting caught in the flight controls; etc... But there is no 'hangar version' of the run-taxi walkaround.  Our training tells us how and why the walkaround inspection is supposed to be done.  If I'd done the proper procedure all of those things would have been caught anyway; and the hammer would certainly have been found before any damage occurred.
column123: On Day 0 at approximately around XB45 (mech )and myself were starting engine 2 on aircraft X. (Mech) was sitting left seat and I was sitting right seat. While the engine was coming up to idle there was a loud bang followed by a severe shutter. I immediately turned off engine 2 while coasting down I monitored the engine for any more issues of which there were none. Soon thereafter multiple mechanics came outside to see what the noise was. Upon inspection there was a hammer found in the inlet that caused considerable visible damage. The hammer was mine and I take full reasonability for putting the hammer it in the inlet and forgetting about it. The reason I put the hammer in the inlet was to stop the fan from wind milling while working on the engine. The fan blades were wind milling at a high speed due a shop fan that I positioned behind the engine to cool down the engine to be able to work on it. After completing my work and putting away my tools I did not perform a proper toolbox inventory nor did I check my immediate area for any loose items. Prior to taking the aircraft out of the hangar I was moving equipment around so it could be taken outside but I did not perform a proper walkaround prior to getting on the aircraft. All of these aforementioned actions after completing my work are a deviation from my normal routines and I have no good reason for this. I did clear engine 2 prior to start but I did not see the hammer most likely due to it being dark as well as its position in the inlet.  Perform an aircraft walk around before Run/taxi actions at all times. Document when non-standard maintenance routines are used.  Use Run/Taxi checklist. Crosscheck performed by both mechanics and a leadership. Use high visibility streamers when there is a chance that tooling may be left on an aircraft

column121: While on an approximate 3-mile final to Runway XX at ZZZ in a Cessna Skyhawk 172S with a pre-solo student pilot; ZZZ Tower cleared a regional jet for takeoff. Departing aircraft was either a Regional Jet CRJ700 or an Embraer 175 E-175. The Tower Controller gave myself and my student the option to either 'extend upwind and expect landing clearance in 3 minutes;' or 'make a full stop taxi-back landing.' I made a transmission stating; 'Full stop taxi-back; Aircraft X.' Then we were cleared for a full stop taxi-back Runway XX. I advised my student we will come in on final approach slightly high and land long; desired touchdown point being the 1;000 ft. white blocks rather than the numbers 'XX.' After our higher-than normal approach to avoid wake turbulence from [the] departing jet and longer-than-normal touchdown point; I had to brake aggressively to make the right turn onto Taxiway XX. My student and I got off the runway; completed the items on the 'after landing' checklist; and then contacted Ground on [frequency]. I felt an abnormal shimmy coming from the nose wheel after letting the airplane slow to a stop on Taxiway XX; holding short of Taxiway XY. We then received our clearance to taxi via Taxiway XY to Runway XX. While holding short Runway XX on Taxiway XY; my student completed the 'pre-takeoff' checklist items and made his radio transmission for 'right closed traffic.' Tower told us to line-up-and-wait Runway XX and he also advised us of traffic coming in on final. I cannot remember if they were 5 miles out or 3 miles. During our takeoff roll I felt a slight shimmy coming from the nose wheel again; same sensation as when we first slowed to a stop while exiting on Taxiway XX. I also noticed our pitch attitude during the takeoff roll was slightly lower than normal. We continued with the takeoff because traffic was close behind us for Runway XX. I did not want to abort the takeoff and make the traffic behind me have to go around; so I decided to have my student continue with the takeoff. After reaching our right downwind leg; we advised Tower we would be making a full stop landing. I advised my student we would be making a soft-field landing; to keep as much weight off the nose wheel for as long as possible; because I suspected an issue with the nosewheel. The soft-field landing was successful; and the nose wheel did not make contact with the ground till rounding the turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. Once back pressure was released and the nose wheel made contact with the ground; the issue became apparent. The nose-wheel tire was completely deflated. Tower then asked if I could make it to the other side of the hold-short lines and I replied that I could and that I would bring the aircraft to a stop on the 'Compass Rose.' Tower then temporarily suspended operations on Runway XX so personnel could make a FOD inspection. Then two firetrucks and two county airport vehicles crossed Runway XX on Taxiway XZ to assist my student and I on the Compass Rose. We then pushed the aircraft to its parking space. A county airport worker called for clearance to cross Taxiway XA before we continued back to our parking space.My personal assessment of the factors leading to the deflated nose wheel tire and the temporary closure of Runway XX. An issue with the ATIS recording at the beginning of the flight was the first abnormality in a series of abnormalities on this flight. During this flight leading up to the events described previously; my student and I were advised to extend upwind and fly runway heading; make right traffic; make a 360; extend our upwind; and finally come in to land. A desire to come in and land after being delayed for so long caused me to make the decision to make the full-stop taxi-back under time-sensitive circumstances; rather than taking Tower's other option presented to me; which was to extend upwind and expect a landing clearance in another 3 minutes.After the full-stop taxi-back and after we were told toline-up-and-wait and that traffic was on final for Runway XX behind us; I decided to commit to the takeoff rather than to abort to prevent the traffic behind me from having to go around; despite my feeling that something was wrong with the nose wheel.Pressure from Tower and the busy environment of the ZZZ airport that day; along with the added pressures and obligations of instructing a pre-solo private pilot student led me to make two errors. Failing to ask to taxi back to our parking space during the initial shimmy experienced on Taxiway XX. Failing to abort the takeoff out of fear of causing an inconvenience to another pilot.Although my student was doing most of the manipulations of the flight controls and making most of the radio calls; I was responsible for the hard-braking to make Taxiway XX; and I was on the controls during the soft-field landing and during the left turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. I was also the pilot-in-command; therefore the responsibilities of this flight were mine; and I should have aborted the takeoff when I suspected an issue with the nose wheel.Traffic pattern was busy; my student and I were only able to make 2 landings with a Hobbs recording of 0.9 hours for the pattern-flight. No one was injured during this flight. Winds were variable during this mishap and weather was not a factor. I am not sick; I am not on any medications; I am not stressed; I have complied with Federal Aviation Regulation (FAR) 91.17; I got well-rested sleep the night before and was not fatigued during the flight; I am emotionally healthy and stable. The aircraft was thoroughly preflighted. All preflight checklists were adhered to and completed; FAR 91.9(a) adhered to.

After contacting the tower and being assigned the route arrival procedure the tower called out traffic for me 1 o'clock altitude unknown.  I told the tower I was searching for the traffic.  The tower told the conflict aircraft my position and they called me insight.  As I continued to search for the traffic an aircraft appeared at my 12 o'clock at extremely close range and my altitude head on.  I had little to no time to react but attempted to push forward and descend and avoid a collision.My aircraft and the conflict traffic collided head on approximately 5 nm north of ZZZ just South of the reporting point [landmark].  My aircraft continued to be controllable and I slowed the aircraft to reduce the risk of structural failure.  I could not see any obvious damage from the cockpit but had heard and felt the impact.  I told the tower I believed I have had a mid air collision and requested the tower to ask the other aircraft if they we OK.  I don't know if anyone responded to the tower.  I continued into ZZZ and landed in the water lane without further incident.  Upon parking the aircraft in the float slip I inspected the aircraft and found minor damage to the right hand fiberglass wingtip from the collision.  No other damage has been discovered at this point.I called the tower on my cell phone and told them I had made contact with the other aircraft.  I then called the FAA and reported the mid air collision.  My aircraft is ADS-B equipped but I believe the other aircraft was not.  I never received any warning on my traffic display and I know it was working from other aircraft warnings on the same flight earlier.  I still do not know the identity of the other aircraft.The area of the [landmark] north of ZZZ is a high traffic area and possible collision risk.  I have operated out of ZZZ for XX plus years without incident.  I believe if the other aircraft had ADS-B and or mode C we could have avoided the collision.  I don't know what could have been done better with the exception of ADS-B on the other aircraft and honestly feel lucky to be alive.

column121: On a typical week-end trip with friends; we wanted a drone shot in a scenic location; so I searched recommended spots and found that Red Rock was a popular spot; confirmed on the map that it was far enough from the airport and that it was far enough from the wilderness area; so we went there. Into the hike we came across a sign indicating that the wilderness area started there; a bit closer than the map seemed to indicate; so we canceled the plan; and I hiked back to the car to put the drone back in the trunk; and we went for the hike again. After the hike; we had such great views that I figured we could still do a panorama shot safely while staying outside the wilderness area. A friend was the designated watcher; and I quickly prepared the drone for a quick shot while our friends waited. I took off and went to a safe altitude of 400 ft.; and started heading towards Red Rock mountain to frame the shot properly. Then the phone screen dimmed suddenly and became harder to read; but I could still clearly see that I was still far from the mountain and the wilderness area; so I headed towards it. What I didn't realize is that the phone had been heat-soaked in the car in the Arizona summer sun all afternoon; and had stopped updating the screen altogether. So while it displayed a picture of the drone safely at a distance; the drone was actually advancing; so I was surprised and confused when the designated watcher called that the drone was out of sight. We talked; and as I went to show him the video feed; the screen went dark. When I turned the phone back on; the connection with the drone was lost.Given last position and direction; it probably crashed near the summit of the Red Rock mountain; hopefully too high to endanger anyone. But it's a touristic wilderness area; so I checked with a ranger who said it was not a problem; that it happens all the time. I'm still worried that the drone likely crashed in a wilderness area; and really hoping it didn't endanger anyone. It's very frustrating as I was trying to do things safely and legally. I should have realized faster that I had lost video feedback and was flying blind. Instead I allowed myself to be distracted by the dimming of the screen. Next time I will pay attention to the heat of course; and should something confusing happen; I will come back and land to sort it out.

column121: On Date; I was doing solo touch-and-go landings at ZZZ. On my fourth lap in the pattern; I lost control of the aircraft after touching down; departed the runway; and struck a taxi sign. I had been out of the cockpit for about two weeks.My final approach was slightly steeper than usual; but I was maintaining my airspeed between 70-75 knots while flying to the numbers; so I decided to continue the approach. As expected; the round-out and flare portion of the landing were longer than usual. In ground effect; the aircraft drifted to the right of the centerline. I corrected this by pointing the nose of the aircraft slightly to the left in order to intercept the runway centerline.As my airspeed slowed past 40; I made contact with the runway and bounced back up into the air. Since a single bounce was not uncommon; my intent at this point was still to continue with the touch-and-go landing.I did one additional bounce as the airplane started coming back towards the runway centerline. I finally lost confidence in the landing and decided to go around. I do not recall precisely the airspeed; but it must have been around 35-40. I began the procedure to wave-off; and I applied full power. By now; the aircraft had settled to the surface and was rolling down the runway.After I increased the throttle to max; I became confused about the next steps to take because I was mentally prepared to execute the touch-and-go; and the actions I was prepared to take were to raise the flaps; turn the carb heat off; and take-off normally.Since the airplane was simply rolling down the runway at this point; I began to do the tasks associated with cleaning up the airplane for a takeoff. I knew that the aircraft would not be able to accelerate well with the flaps in the landing configuration; so I reached over and began to raise the flaps. I also needed to turn the carb heat off. But I was unfamiliar with the flap selector switch on this aircraft; since it was a spring-loaded switch. When I took my hand off of it to turn the carb heat off; the flaps stopped moving. I returned my hand to the flap selector again to raise the flaps and looked around to verify the physical position of the flaps.Throughout this entire time; I had been rolling from the right side of the runway back towards the centerline. Also; due to being at full power; the left-turning tendency of the airplane caused it to veer to the left. Since I was fixated on the flaps and preoccupied with the switches in the cockpit and checking the flap position; I did not immediately notice the change in airplane's direction. When I looked ahead again; I had only had a few hundred feet remaining before departing off the left side of the runway.At this point; I remember feeling confused because I was halfway through the procedures for a touch-and-go and halfway through the procedures for a go around. I was not completely confident in the ability to rotate and take off because the flaps were still partially retracted and I was unsure of the airspeed that I had. I knew for certain that I wanted to avoid any possibility of a low-level stall; so I wanted to abort the takeoff.I took out the power and applied right rudder and braking in attempt to stay on the hard surface; but did not do so aggressively enough to make a meaningful change in direction. I briefly considered applying even more right rudder and right brake pressures; but I am unfamiliar with the ground handling characteristics at high speed and did not want to risk tipping over the airplane and causing a wingtip strike.I believed that the best course of action was to slow down straight ahead. My first reaction was to apply full braking; but I ended up skidding and suddenly veering further left; directly towards the taxi sign. After knocking down the sign; I braked and came to a stop in the grass between the taxiway and runway. Then; I immediately proceeded with the emergency engine shutdown checklist.

column121: While practicing ground control and taxing on RWY XX at 30 MPH; maintaining centerline with nose wheel raised. The aircraft began to lift off; I reduced power and added up elevator then applied additional power to slow settling. I over controlled both power and elevator resulting in pilot induced oscillation (porpoising). The aircraft impacted the nose wheel twice with the second impact resulting in collapse of the nose gear. The propeller struck the runway then the right-wing tip drug followed by the left-wing tip. I called tower to request assistance and let them know that I the single occupant had sustained no injuries. I turned off all fuel; power and ignition then unbuckled and exited the aircraft. I picked up the pieces of the damaged propeller and by pushing the tail down was able to push the aircraft off the active runway on its mains. I then waited for assistance to arrive. The weather at the time was wind calm; sky clear with reported visibility reported better than 10 miles.

column121: During climb out; FA (Flight Attendant) called on intercom to report a very loud banging noise behind the wing area; aircraft right side; row 31. FA said it sounded like someone pounding on the fuselage with a sledgehammer repeatedly. We leveled off at FL280 immediately and reduced speed from 280 KIAS to 250 KIAS. I asked the FO to look for a nearby field with good weather.  FA recorded the noise via video on her cell phone and brought it to the cockpit. After reviewing the video; we decided to divert to ZZZ. We notified dispatch and coordinated with the FA's and informed the passengers. During the descent and configuration of the aircraft for landing at ZZZ; with the flaps at 5deg; I called for Flaps 10 while the aircraft speed was at 209 KIAS. I immediately said 'delay that stay at flaps five.' I believe the FO moved the flap handle out of the 5 detent and returned it immediately. The flaps remained at 5 degrees and I continued to slow the aircraft. I called for gear down an Flaps 15; flaps 25; flaps 30 landing checklist. I noticed the stick shaker indicator on the airspeed tape was in an unusual position and cross checked the configuration to find the flaps were at 5. We were at approximately 1200 feet when I announced 'going around'; but did not hit TOGA as I did not want GA thrust. At this point; the FO and I were convinced that the two problems were related; that there was some structural damage to the flaps.We climbed to 5;000 feet and referenced the Checklist for FLAPS - TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE. We returned the flap lever to 5; then selected 2. The flaps retracted to 2. The checklist directed us to 'Proceed normally.' We had a discussion about what that meant and were not comfortable with extending the flaps again; with suspected mechanical damage to the flaps already existing. We got a phone patch with Maintenance Control and dispatch on HF and discussed the two issues and our checklist. They had no additional advice. We discussed the plan to land in the current flap configuration (flap 2); using the flap up speeds with Maintenance Control and dispatch. The FO had already assessed the landing distance and we referenced the FLAPS- TRAILING EDGE FLAPS UP LANDING checklist. We landed on RWY XXL at ZZZ; at VREF 40 + 40 + 5. I used auto brakes 3; and rolled to the end of the runway. We had the fire/rescue look us over for damage prior to proceeding to the gate. They reported a large cable hanging from the satellite antenna. The PSEU (Proximity Switch Electronics Unit) light came on after landing. The FO and I debriefed the events in detail post flight and during the next two flights. It was not until the following morning; that I realized that in all likelihood; I caused the flap malfunction by calling for flaps 10 at 209 KIAS. The SATCOM antenna seal failure noise was significantly concerning; and I assumed the flap issue was directly related.
